m1-l1.title: Set up Scratch and your paper toolkit
m1-l1.summary: Gather a pencil, paper, and a few things from around the house, open the free Scratch editor, and decide with a grown-up whether you want a Scratch account.
m1-l1.module: Get ready to think like a programmer

m1-l2.title: Run your first algorithm and prove it works
m1-l2.summary: Write four plain-English steps, turn them into a Scratch script, predict what will happen, and check the result against your prediction.

m1-l3.title: Save your work, keep a notebook, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Save and reload Scratch projects, name your files so you can find them, set up an algorithm notebook page, and learn a routine for when nothing works.

m2-l1.title: Break a problem into goals, inputs, and smaller pieces
m2-l1.summary: Describe a messy problem by its goal, inputs, constraints, and output, split it into pieces small enough to solve, and spot the pieces that repeat.
m2-l1.module: Break big problems into small ones

m2-l2.title: Build a fair-share helper for the computer lab
m2-l2.summary: Plan a Scratch program as four separate pieces, build and test each piece on its own, and check the finished helper with tricky inputs.

m2-l3.title: Practice: pizza orders, pet sitters, and a bake sale
m2-l3.summary: Name the goal, inputs, constraints, and output of everyday problems, decompose a morning routine and a game, fix fuzzy instructions, and extend the fair-share helper in Scratch.

m3-l1.title: Write instructions a robot can't misread
m3-l1.summary: Learn what turns a list of steps into an algorithm, track a robot's position and direction as each step runs, name inputs and outputs, and find ambiguous steps by acting them out.

m3-l2.title: Program a delivery robot to cross the room
m3-l2.summary: Plan a route around an obstacle as numbered steps, check it with a state table, then build it in Scratch with a starting state, visible moves, and a second event that resets the robot.

m3-l3.title: Practice: robot routes, scrambled steps, and drawing blind
m3-l3.summary: Order scrambled steps, trace and write grid-robot routes, name inputs and outputs, fix a Scratch script that fails on its second run, and write drawing instructions a partner can follow without peeking.

m4-l1.title: Spot patterns and let loops do the repeating
m4-l1.summary: Find the part of a task that repeats, replace repeated steps with a loop, choose between counting loops and condition-controlled loops, and decide which steps belong inside the loop.
m4-l1.module: Spot patterns and repeat with loops

m4-l2.title: Draw a flower of squares with loops
m4-l2.summary: Use Scratch's Pen extension to draw a square the long way, shrink it with a loop, turn it into any shape by changing one number, repeat it into a twelve-petal flower, and draw a spiral that stops at the edge.

m4-l3.title: Practice: dances, label printers, staircases, and countdowns
m4-l3.summary: Compress repeated steps into loops, sort steps into before, inside, and after, choose counting or condition-controlled loops, predict nested loops, and draw and count with loops in Scratch.

m5-l1.title: Decisions with if/else, and/or, and the edge cases that break them
m5-l1.summary: Turn rules into true-or-false conditions, choose a path with if/else, combine checks with and, or, and not, and test the boundary values where rules go wrong.
m5-l1.module: Make decisions and handle edge cases

m5-l2.title: Build a library checkout kiosk in Scratch
m5-l2.summary: Build a Scratch kiosk that asks four questions, applies the library's borrowing rules in order, explains every "no," and passes a full table of edge-case tests.

m5-l3.title: Decision practice: tickets, rides, rock-paper-scissors, and leap years
m5-l3.summary: Solve six decision problems in Scratch, from ticket prices to leap years, and find the edge cases that break each rule.

m6-l1.title: Find bugs by predicting, tracing, and testing
m6-l1.summary: Compare what a script should do with what it really does, trace it by hand, spot the three places bugs hide, and use a step-by-step routine to fix them for good.

m6-l2.title: Debug a weekend-proof alarm clock in Scratch
m6-l2.summary: Build Sam's buggy alarm clock with a test mode, write a test plan, then track down a condition bug, an order bug, and a loop bug one at a time.

m6-l3.title: Bug hunt practice: trace, test, and fix six broken scripts
m6-l3.summary: Trace scripts by hand, design tests that expose hidden bugs, and fix sequence, condition, and loop errors in six short Scratch scripts and a three-bug challenge.

m7-l1.title: Compare algorithms by counting steps
m7-l1.summary: Compare linear search, binary search, and selection sort by counting their steps, and see why halving beats checking one at a time as lists grow.

m7-l2.title: Build a number-guessing robot that uses binary search
m7-l2.summary: Build a Scratch robot that finds your secret number from 1 to 100 in at most 7 guesses, catches players who change their number, and proves it beats counting up.

m7-l3.title: Algorithm showdown: searches, sorts, mazes, and a fake coin
m7-l3.summary: Count the steps of searches and sorts by hand, race two sorting algorithms on the same cards, test a maze-solving rule until it fails, and solve a balance-scale puzzle in two weighings.

m8-l1.title: Choose your capstone and plan the algorithm
m8-l1.summary: Pick a capstone project (a maze, a puzzle, a sorting task, or a real-world process), then plan its inputs, outputs, steps, decisions, loops, edge cases, and tests before building anything.
m8-l1.module: Capstone: design and defend an algorithm

m8-l2.title: Build your capstone in milestones
m8-l2.summary: Build your capstone in six milestones, each ending with something that runs and a test it passes, using the change maker as a worked example and starter scripts for every project idea.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your capstone
m8-l3.summary: Run a final test day and a break-it round, polish your Scratch project, explain your algorithm in three minutes, check your work against the rubric, and take your first look at a text language.

m1-l1.title: Get Scratch running on your computer
m1-l1.summary: Pick the online editor or the free Scratch app, open it on Windows, macOS, a Chromebook, or Linux, and decide with a parent whether you want an account.
m1-l1.module: Get Scratch ready

m1-l2.title: Prove your setup works with a systems-check project
m1-l2.summary: Learn where everything lives in the Scratch editor, then build five tiny tests for the green flag, keyboard, mouse, and speakers, and save and reopen the project to prove saving works.

m1-l3.title: Save your work, keep it organized, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Learn how the course's modules fit together, set up a saving and naming routine that protects your projects, carry code between projects, and follow a step-by-step routine when a script misbehaves.

m2-l1.title: The stage grid, costumes, and the events that start scripts
m2-l1.summary: Place sprites exactly with x and y coordinates, aim them with directions, change how they look with costumes, backdrops, and layers, and start scripts with event hat blocks that run side by side.

m2-l2.title: Build Firefly Night, a scene you catch with the mouse
m2-l2.summary: Paint a two-costume firefly, make five of them wander and blink inside a band of night sky, catch them in a jar with a click, and bring on the morning with one broadcast.

m2-l3.title: Practice: coordinates, directions, layers, and events
m2-l3.summary: Predict and measure sprite positions, test how far Scratch lets a sprite go past the edge, steer a character that faces the way it walks, fix layer order and a runaway animation, switch scenes with backdrop events, and build a mirror twin.

m3-l1.title: Broadcasts, variables, and game states
m3-l1.summary: Replace fragile wait timers with broadcast messages, control order with broadcast and wait, store scores and modes in variables, and use conditions and a state variable to decide what a game does next.

m3-l2.title: Build a two-player key-mash race with a fair start
m3-l2.summary: Build a race where two players hammer the A and L keys, with a referee who waits for both racers to reach the line, a countdown nobody can time, false-start penalties, exactly one winner per round, and a first-to-three scoreboard.

m3-l3.title: Practice: broadcasts, scores, and game states
m3-l3.summary: Predict message timing, replace guessed waits with broadcasts, score gifts by costume, give three ghosts their own health, add a pause key, rescue a frozen title screen, build a combo meter, and code rock, paper, scissors.

m4-l1.title: Game feel: frames, easing, animation, sound, and fair rules
m4-l1.summary: Learn how Scratch's 30-frames-a-second loop turns numbers into motion, make sprites ease toward a target, time animations and sounds so they never freeze a game, use graphic effects as feedback, and write scoring and edge rules players can trust.

m4-l2.title: Build Reef Catch, a catch game with juice
m4-l2.summary: Build an underwater catch game where a crab eases after the mouse, snaps its claws only while moving, catches sinking starfish for points and a rising chime, dodges jellyfish aimed at it, and plays out a clear game over.

m4-l3.title: Practice: motion, animation, sound, and fair feedback
m4-l3.summary: Work out speeds in frames, wrap sprites around the stage, time a walk cycle with a frame counter, make a line of chicks ease after the mouse, give a player two seconds of safety after a hit, fix a sound that freezes a pickup, bounce a ball with velocity, and build a rhythm game.

m5-l1.title: Make sprites bump, land, and stay on the stage
m5-l1.summary: Pick the right touch-sensing block, stop players at walls with move-check-undo, add gravity and jumping with a speed variable, and keep sprites from vanishing off the stage.

m5-l2.title: Build Crystal Climb, a platformer with gravity and jumping
m5-l2.summary: Paint a level, then code a player that walks, falls, lands, jumps only from the ground, bonks its head on ceilings, respawns from pits, and wins by reaching a crystal.

m5-l3.title: Practice: spikes, coins, guards, and double jumps
m5-l3.summary: Add hazards, pickups, a guard with a sight range, a bounce pad, wall sliding, and a double jump to your platformer, then try momentum and ice as a challenge.

m6-l1.title: Make many objects with clones, custom blocks, and lists
m6-l1.summary: Spawn and manage copies of a sprite with clones, give each clone its own memory, name reusable code with My Blocks, make loops finish instantly with run without screen refresh, and store many values in a list.

m6-l2.title: Build Ghost Patrol, a lane shooter made of clones
m6-l2.summary: Build a four-lane shooter where a wizard hops between lanes stored in a list, casts spark clones, and fights ghost clones that each have their own speed, using custom blocks for spawning and vanishing.

m6-l3.title: Practice: clone swarms, particle bursts, and a high-score table
m6-l3.summary: Fix a clone explosion, give clones their own speeds, build custom blocks with inputs, land Pip pixel-perfectly with run without screen refresh, and keep a sorted top-5 list.

m7-l1.title: Plan game states, levels, and difficulty that adapts
m7-l1.summary: Map a multi-level game as states, load each level safely with broadcast and wait, store level settings in lists, shape a difficulty curve with rests, and nudge the difficulty to match the player.

m7-l2.title: Give Ghost Patrol a story, five waves, and difficulty that adapts
m7-l2.summary: Turn the Module 6 shooter into a complete game with a title screen, a short story, five waves read from lists, a rest wave, win and lose endings, and ghost speed that adjusts to how well you play.

m7-l3.title: Practice: branching stories, adaptive quizzes, and level systems
m7-l3.summary: Fix a clone pile-up between levels, build a story that handles any answer, design a curve with rests, write a quiz that adapts, give Crystal Climb three levels, and code a rival that rubber-bands.

m8-l1.title: Plan your multi-level Scratch game
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, pick one of five game ideas (or your own) at the right difficulty, and fill in a one-page plan with states, sprites, variables, levels, and a must-have list.

m8-l2.title: Build your game in milestones, starting from a skeleton
m8-l2.summary: Start from a skeleton that already runs title, levels, and endings, then add the player, goals, clones, difficulty, and feedback one tested milestone at a time, using a three-level Crystal Climb as the worked example.

m8-l3.title: Playtest, polish, and present your game
m8-l3.summary: Run a written test plan, watch a real player without helping, fix problems in the right order, add polish that makes the game feel alive, write the project page, present it in two minutes, and check it against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Install Thonny and check that Python works
m1-l1.summary: Download Thonny, which brings its own copy of Python, on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook, open it for the first time, and type one line that proves it works.
m1-l1.module: Set up Thonny and run Python

m1-l2.title: Write, save, and run your first Thonny program
m1-l2.summary: Type a four-line program in Thonny's editor, save it as a .py file in a course folder, run it, step through it one line at a time, and break it on purpose to meet your first error messages.

m1-l3.title: How to work in this course, keep your files tidy, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Learn how each module's three lessons fit together, set up a folder and naming scheme that won't break your programs, read an error message from the bottom up, and follow a routine for when you're stuck.

m2-l1.title: Store and track values with variables
m2-l1.summary: Give values names with variables, update them as a program runs, tell text, whole numbers, decimals, and True/False apart, and watch every value change in Thonny's Variables panel.

m2-l2.title: Build a status tracker for a text adventure
m2-l2.summary: Write a short text adventure that keeps a hero's health, gold, bag weight, and key in variables, prints a status line after every scene, and uses Thonny's Variables panel to catch a planted bug.

m2-l3.title: Practice: track values, fix name errors, and swap variables
m2-l3.summary: Trace variables by hand, repair NameErrors, swap and rotate values, keep a running balance, find a silent bug with the debugger, and run a scoreboard that recalculates as it goes.

m3-l1.title: Text, numbers, and what input() really gives you
m3-l1.summary: Slice and clean text with string methods, convert what people type into numbers with int() and float(), get True/False answers about text, and format output exactly with f-strings.
m3-l1.module: Work with text, numbers, input, and output

m3-l2.title: Build a club sign-up slip that cleans up messy answers
m3-l2.summary: Write a sign-up program that asks seven questions, tidies whatever people type with string methods, converts numbers, builds a member code from slices, and prints an aligned confirmation slip with f-strings.

m3-l3.title: Practice: slice text, convert input, and format output
m3-l3.summary: Predict string results, print a name badge with initials, fix a program that crashes on decimals, line up a results table, build usernames from slices, estimate download times, and draw a banner sized to fit any message.

m4-l1.title: Calculate, compare, and decide with if, elif, and else
m4-l1.summary: Use all seven arithmetic operators, compare values to get True or False, make a program choose between paths with if, elif, and else, combine conditions with and, or, and not, and test the edges where decision bugs hide.

m4-l2.title: Build a bike-share fare calculator
m4-l2.summary: Turn a page of pricing rules into a program that charges each rider correctly, using arithmetic, if/elif/else, and conditions joined with and, then check it with boundary tests at every cutoff.

m4-l3.title: Practice: calculate, decide, and test the edges
m4-l3.summary: Split eggs into cartons with // and %, solve FizzBuzz for one number, apply a pool's swim rules with and and or, turn Wi-Fi signal strength into bars, price shipping, fix a discount bug with boundary tests, and convert 24-hour times.

m5-l1.title: Repeat work with while and for loops
m5-l1.summary: Use while loops to keep asking until an answer is valid, for loops to walk through ranges and lists, running totals to add things up, and break and continue to steer a loop.

m5-l2.title: Build a mental math sprint with loops
m5-l2.summary: Build a five-question multiplication quiz that rejects bad answers, keeps score, and lets the player skip or quit, using for, while, break, and continue.

m5-l3.title: Practice loops with ratings, playlists, and hailstone numbers
m5-l3.summary: Solve six loop problems, from counting down by twos to the doubling-penny puzzle, then trace the strange path of hailstone numbers in a challenge.

m6-l1.title: Write your own functions with def and return
m6-l1.summary: Package repeated code into functions, pass values in with parameters, send results back with return, keep variables local, and describe each function with a docstring.

m6-l2.title: Build a race pace calculator from small functions
m6-l2.summary: Build a running pace calculator out of six small functions, test each one on its own, fix a float formatting bug, and reuse a validation function for every question.

m6-l3.title: Practice writing and fixing functions
m6-l3.summary: Write six functions that return useful values, from initials to a text progress bar, fix a print-instead-of-return bug and a scope bug, then build a secret-message cipher.

m7-l1.title: Read tracebacks, handle errors, and store app data
m7-l1.summary: Read a Python traceback from the bottom up, recognize the eight errors beginners meet most, catch expected errors with try and except, follow a debugging routine, and keep app data in lists and dictionaries.
m7-l1.module: Read errors and build small apps

m7-l2.title: Build a virtual pet game with a dictionary and a menu
m7-l2.summary: Assemble a complete text game from a dictionary of pet stats, small action functions, a validated menu loop, and win and lose rules, fixing a KeyError along the way.

m7-l3.title: Practice debugging and organizing app data
m7-l3.summary: Read tracebacks, fix name, type, index, and logic bugs in short programs, validate prices with try and except, and use dictionaries to run a snack shop, count words, and keep an arcade high-score table.

m8-l1.title: Plan your capstone text app
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone requirements, choose one of six project ideas (or your own), write a sample session, and plan your data and functions before writing any code.

m8-l2.title: Build your capstone in five milestones
m8-l2.summary: Start from a runnable skeleton, grow your app through five milestones that each end with working code, and follow a small text adventure built exactly that way.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your capstone
m8-l3.summary: Test your app with a table of normal, edge, and nasty inputs, let Python check your functions automatically, polish the code, write a README, give a two-minute demo, and score your work against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Install Python, VS Code, and the Python extension
m1-l1.summary: Install Python 3 and Visual Studio Code on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook, add Microsoft's Python extension, and confirm all three work together from VS Code's terminal.
m1-l1.module: Set up VS Code for Python

m1-l2.title: Run your first file and give the project its own Python
m1-l2.summary: Open a project folder in VS Code, run a Python file with the Run button and from the terminal, then create a .venv virtual environment and prove your code runs inside it.

m1-l3.title: Organize your project folder and get unstuck fast
m1-l3.summary: Set up one folder per module, name files so Python never confuses them with its own modules, read a traceback from the bottom up, and follow a four-step routine when code breaks.

m2-l1.title: Model records with lists and dicts, then reshape them
m2-l1.summary: Store related values together in lists of dictionaries, pick the right collection for each job, walk nested data, and build new lists and orderings with comprehensions and sorted(key=...).

m2-l2.title: Build a grade book that turns raw text into a ranked report
m2-l2.summary: Parse messy comma-separated scores into records, group them by student, compute averages and letter grades with comprehensions, and print a ranked, aligned report.

m2-l3.title: Count, group, filter, and sort real data
m2-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on word counts, unique tags, filtered task lists, multi-field sorting, inverted dictionaries, and study-log totals, ending with a study planner's data model.

m3-l1.title: Untangle nested logic with guard clauses and small functions
m3-l1.summary: Read loops and conditions nested several levels deep, flatten them with guard clauses, return values instead of printing them, split big functions into small ones, and understand where each variable lives.
m3-l1.module: Write small functions with clear jobs

m3-l2.title: Build a contacts manager from small, testable functions
m3-l2.summary: Build a command-line contacts manager where each function has one job (cleaning phone numbers, checking emails, adding, searching, deleting) and only the menu talks to the user.

m3-l3.title: Refactor tangled code into functions that return answers
m3-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on fixing print-instead-of-return bugs, flattening nested ifs with guard clauses, separating calculation from display, repairing scope errors, comparing every pair in a list, and splitting a report generator into testable parts.

m4-l1.title: Save and load data with text files, JSON, and pathlib
m4-l1.summary: Make a program remember things between runs by writing text and JSON files with `with open`, handling missing and corrupt files without losing data, and building paths with pathlib.
m4-l1.module: Save data to text and JSON files

m4-l2.title: Build a quiz game that loads questions and saves scores as JSON
m4-l2.summary: Build a terminal quiz that reads its questions from a JSON file, rejects broken questions with clear warnings, and keeps a score history in a second JSON file that survives crashes and corruption.

m4-l3.title: Make programs remember with text and JSON files
m4-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on journals, file statistics, number keys and sets in JSON, a persistent expense tracker, per-month files found with pathlib, and saving the contacts manager to disk.

m5-l1.title: Import modules and refuse bad input
m5-l1.summary: Use import to pull in the standard library and your own files, explain why a script breaks on someone else's computer, and write input checks that ask again instead of crashing.

m5-l2.title: Build a times-table drill with random, argparse, and Counter
m5-l2.summary: Build a command-line multiplication drill that picks random questions, refuses non-numbers without marking them wrong, takes options like --count and --seed, and tells you which facts to practice.

m5-l3.title: Practice imports, dates, and input that asks again
m5-l3.summary: Solve six problems with random, datetime, collections, and argparse, write validators for yes/no answers and dates, then build a menu loop that never crashes on bad input.

m6-l1.title: Find bugs with evidence instead of guesses
m6-l1.summary: Read a traceback from the bottom up, print values in a way that shows the truth, make code check itself with assert, switch noisy prints to logging, and shrink a bug to a few lines.

m6-l2.title: Track down a sold-out bug with the VS Code debugger
m6-l2.summary: Reproduce an inventory bug that only shows up on some days, pause the program with breakpoints, watch the list change as you step, prove the cause in the Debug Console, then fix it and add a check that keeps it fixed.

m6-l3.title: Practice debugging tracebacks, silent bugs, and shared lists
m6-l3.summary: Find and fix seven bugs using tracebacks, f-string prints, repr, logging, a conditional breakpoint, and a minimal reproduction, ending with a shared-data bug that breaks undo.

m7-l1.title: Design a command-line tool before you build it
m7-l1.summary: Plan a multi-feature program by writing its commands first, split it into interface, logic, and storage layers, route subcommands through one main() function, and report errors with exit codes and a README.

m7-l2.title: Build a reading log with subcommands and JSON storage
m7-l2.summary: Build shelf.py, a reading tracker with add, read, list, and stats commands, split into storage, logic, and interface files, with clear errors, exit codes, and a README.

m7-l3.title: Practice planning, splitting, and wiring up command-line tools
m7-l3.summary: Design a tool from its commands, untangle a function into logic and interface, add subcommands, test main() through exit codes, harden a loader, write a README, and add a CSV export to the reading log.

m8-l1.title: Plan your persistent productivity tool
m8-l1.summary: Pick a capstone project, from a to-do list to a gear-checkout system, and plan it on one page with its commands, data shape, layers, hard parts, and milestones before writing code.

m8-l2.title: Build the habit tracker in five milestones
m8-l2.summary: Build the capstone example milestone by milestone, from crash-safe JSON storage to check-ins, streak math with datetime, and a full argparse command line, then split it into three files.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your tool
m8-l3.summary: Turn your plan's examples into unittest tests, watch a test catch a real bug, test whole commands through main(), polish messages and the README, then demo the tool and grade it against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Install Python, VS Code, and the Python extension
m1-l1.summary: Install Python 3, VS Code, and Microsoft's Python extension on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook, then run a short script that proves all three are connected.
m1-l1.module: Get set up with VS Code, Python, and pytest

m1-l2.title: Make a virtual environment and pass your first pytest test
m1-l2.summary: Give your project its own virtual environment, install pytest into it, write two tests for a withdraw function, and watch them pass, fail, and pass again.

m1-l3.title: Organize your project, read tracebacks, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Set up one folder per module, split code from its tests, read a traceback from the bottom up, watch variables change in the VS Code debugger, and follow a routine when you're stuck.

m2-l1.title: Classes, instances, and the self that ties them together
m2-l1.summary: See why parallel lists break, then write a class, create instances with their own attributes, call methods that change their state, and understand exactly what self is.

m2-l2.title: Build a bank Account class with history and transfers
m2-l2.summary: Turn a parallel-list bank script into an Account class that validates every change, records its own history, prints a statement, and moves money safely between accounts, with tests.

m2-l3.title: Practice: counters, stock levels, and library copies
m2-l3.summary: Write six small classes whose state changes through methods, from a click counter to library book copies on a shelf, then build members who borrow copies without the two sides ever disagreeing.

m3-l1.title: Constructors, class attributes, and has-a versus is-a
m3-l1.summary: Write constructors that validate and use safe defaults, share values with class attributes, extend a class with inheritance and super(), and decide when composition is the better relationship.

m3-l2.title: Grow the bank with numbered accounts, a Bank, and savings
m3-l2.summary: Extend the bank with transaction objects, auto-numbered accounts, a Bank that composes them, and a SavingsAccount built with inheritance, then run month-end for every account without a single type check.

m3-l3.title: Practice: constructors, delivery vehicles, and route planning
m3-l3.summary: Fix shared defaults, number objects with class attributes, add an alternative constructor, then build a delivery fleet with inheritance and a route planner with composition.

m4-l1.title: Properties, dunder methods, dataclasses, and type hints
m4-l1.summary: Hide internal state behind a clear interface with underscores and @property, make objects print and compare sensibly with dunder methods, cut boilerplate with @dataclass, and say what types you mean with hints.

m4-l2.title: Harden the bank behind a clear interface
m4-l2.summary: Rebuild the bank so balances and histories can only change through methods, transactions are frozen dataclasses, bad amounts are refused at the door, and the Bank works with len, in, and for loops.

m4-l3.title: Practice: properties, value objects, and a small inventory
m4-l3.summary: Guard values with properties, fix dataclass defaults, sort a shelf, build a Money value object, make a library collection work with len and in, let type hints expose a None bug, then build a tested inventory system.

m5-l1.title: Raise, catch, and name your own exceptions
m5-l1.summary: Read a traceback, catch only the errors you can handle, build an exception hierarchy for a booking app, and split the code into modules with a __main__ guard.

m5-l2.title: Build a booking package with its own error types
m5-l2.summary: Split a hotel booking app into a package of modules, give it a custom exception hierarchy, and write a menu that reports every booking problem clearly without hiding real bugs.

m5-l3.title: Practice catching, raising, and organizing errors
m5-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on narrow except clauses, validation in constructors, exception hierarchies, raise from, retries, and the __main__ guard.

m6-l1.title: Interfaces, polymorphism, and tests that hold them to their word
m6-l1.summary: Use duck typing and abc.ABC to define interfaces, call many classes through one method name, and write pytest and unittest tests, with fixtures and fakes, that prove a reusable component works.

m6-l2.title: Build a reusable DateRange component, test first
m6-l2.summary: Write the tests before the code to build a small DateRange class that any project can import, catch a boundary bug the moment it appears, and run the finished suite with pytest.

m6-l3.title: Practice interfaces, fakes, and test-first code
m6-l3.summary: Replace if/elif chains with polymorphic classes, define an ABC with two real implementations, find a bug by writing tests, test with fakes, and make a given test suite pass.

m7-l1.title: Code smells, safe refactoring, and SOLID in small examples
m7-l1.summary: Recognize the code smells that make changes risky, refactor in small test-protected steps with extract function and extract class, and see each SOLID principle in a few lines of Python.

m7-l2.title: Refactor a tangled store checkout without breaking it
m7-l2.summary: Pin a legacy checkout function with characterization tests, then extract functions, an Inventory class, polymorphic discount rules, and an injectable Checkout, rerunning the tests after every step.

m7-l3.title: Practice refactoring with tests as your safety net
m7-l3.summary: Name the numbers, introduce parameter objects, replace conditionals with classes, fix a Liskov violation, inject randomness, and pin down legacy code you don't understand before cleaning it up.

m8-l1.title: Plan an object-oriented application you'll actually finish
m8-l1.summary: Pick a capstone project, find its classes from a written scenario, draw the class diagram, justify every relationship, write the acceptance test that defines "done", and fill in a design document.
m8-l1.module: Capstone: design, build, and explain an application

m8-l2.title: Build the capstone in milestones, starting from a working engine
m8-l2.summary: Grow a text adventure engine milestone by milestone, from rooms loaded from data to a player, command classes, locked doors, and a win condition, with tests passing at the end of every stage.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your capstone
m8-l3.summary: Write a test plan that covers every class and error path, test the whole program with scripted input, polish the code and design document, give a five-minute demo, and check your work against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Install VS Code, Live Server, and a browser with DevTools
m1-l1.summary: Set up the free tools for this course on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook, or use CodePen if you can't install anything.
m1-l1.module: Set up your web workshop

m1-l2.title: Make your first page and inspect it with DevTools
m1-l2.summary: Create index.html in VS Code, serve it with Live Server, watch it reload on save, and edit it live in the browser's Elements panel.

m1-l3.title: Organize your files, save safely, and debug a broken page
m1-l3.summary: Set up a tidy folder for each project, name files so they survive being published, and follow a step-by-step routine when a page looks wrong.

m2-l1.title: How a browser turns your HTML into a page
m2-l1.summary: Follow a page from request to pixels, then write the skeleton, headings, paragraphs, links, and images that every web page is made of.

m2-l2.title: Build a two-page personal profile site
m2-l2.summary: Build a profile page with a photo, a heading outline, jump links, outside links, and a second page in a subfolder that links back.

m2-l3.title: Repair skeletons, outline headings, and trace file paths
m2-l3.summary: Fix broken pages, choose heading levels, write alt text, work out relative paths, and build a one-page fan site with jump links.

m3-l1.title: Give content meaning with landmarks, lists, tables, and forms
m3-l1.summary: Mark up page regions, lists, data tables, and accessible forms with the elements that tell browsers and screen readers what each part is.

m3-l2.title: Mark up a recipe page with landmarks, lists, and a table
m3-l2.summary: Build a complete recipe page with a header and navigation, an article with a captioned photo, an at-a-glance table, ingredient and method lists, a tips aside, and a footer.

m3-l3.title: Rewrite div soup, build tables, and fix inaccessible forms
m3-l3.summary: Replace generic divs with landmarks, choose and nest lists, build a schedule table, repair a broken form, and build an event registration form from scratch.

m4-l1.title: Selectors, the cascade, specificity, and the box model
m4-l1.summary: Write CSS rules, target elements with selectors, predict which rule wins a conflict, and work out exactly how big every box on the page is.

m4-l2.title: Style a sign-up form card with selectors and the box model
m4-l2.summary: Write the HTML for an accessible sign-up form, link a stylesheet, and style it into a centered card, fixing real specificity and box-sizing bugs along the way.

m4-l3.title: Predict the cascade, score specificity, and measure boxes
m4-l3.summary: Write precise selectors, rank selectors by specificity, calculate box sizes, debug CSS that won't apply, fix spacing, and style a profile card to an exact spec.

m5-l1.title: Line things up with Flexbox and Grid
m5-l1.summary: Use Flexbox to arrange items along one line and Grid to place them in rows and columns, with gap, wrapping, fr units, repeat(), minmax(), and named areas.
m5-l1.module: Lay out pages with Flexbox and Grid

m5-l2.title: Build a product card grid for an online snack shop
m5-l2.summary: Build a shop page whose product cards line up in as many columns as fit, with buttons pinned to the bottom of every card and a Flexbox toolbar on top.

m5-l3.title: Practice: navbars, galleries, and page layouts
m5-l3.summary: Six layout exercises that get harder as you go, from centering a badge to building a dashboard, plus a calendar challenge built with CSS Grid.

m6-l1.title: Make a page work on a phone and with a keyboard
m6-l1.summary: Use the viewport tag, flexible units, clamp(), mobile-first media queries, and scaling images, then fix the contrast, focus, keyboard, and motion problems that lock visitors out.

m6-l2.title: Build a responsive, accessible landing page
m6-l2.summary: Build a one-page site for a stargazing club that starts as a phone layout, grows into two columns on wider screens, and works with a keyboard from the first Tab.

m6-l3.title: Practice: fix pages that break on phones and keyboards
m6-l3.summary: Six repair jobs on broken pages, from sideways scrolling and frozen font sizes to missing focus rings, weak contrast, and fake buttons, plus a responsive gallery challenge.

m7-l1.title: Make several pages look like one site
m7-l1.summary: Build visual hierarchy with type, spacing, and color, store design decisions in CSS custom properties, and connect pages with relative links and one shared stylesheet.

m7-l2.title: Build a three-page club site with one shared stylesheet
m7-l2.summary: Build a home page, an events page, and a sign-up page for a robotics club that share one stylesheet of design tokens, one header, and working relative links.

m7-l3.title: Practice: tokens, hierarchy, and paths between pages
m7-l3.summary: Six exercises on custom properties, visual hierarchy, spacing, relative paths, and themes, plus a challenge to build a style guide page from your own design tokens.

m8-l1.title: Plan your capstone: a responsive multi-page website
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, choose a site idea that fits your skills, and plan it with a sitemap, real content, phone-first wireframes, and design tokens before writing any code.

m8-l2.title: Build your capstone in milestones, then publish it on GitHub Pages
m8-l2.summary: Start from a working skeleton, build your site in six milestones that each end with something you can check, and publish it free at a real address with GitHub Pages.

m8-l3.title: Finish your capstone: test, polish, present, and keep going
m8-l3.summary: Test your live site at five widths, with the keyboard, at 200% zoom, and with automated checkers, write up one bug you fixed, polish the details, present it, and see how it will be graded.

m1-l1.title: Install VS Code, Live Server, and a browser console
m1-l1.summary: Install the free VS Code editor and its Live Server extension on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook, make a course folder, and get the browser Console to answer you.
m1-l1.module: Set up your JavaScript workspace

m1-l2.title: Link your first script and build a click counter
m1-l2.summary: Create index.html and script.js, connect them with a deferred script tag, prove it with console.log, and make a button that counts its clicks.

m1-l3.title: Read errors, save often, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Organize one folder per project, make sure your saves reach the browser, decode the Console's most common error messages, and follow a routine when code won't work.

m2-l1.title: Model a reading list with values, arrays, objects, and functions
m2-l1.summary: Learn JavaScript's building blocks (types, let and const, strings, numbers, arrays, objects, and functions) by modelling a reading tracker, and use console.log to check each step.

m2-l2.title: Build a tip calculator that splits the bill
m2-l2.summary: Write a calculateTip function step by step, fix the string and decimal bugs that real form input causes, round money in whole cents, and connect it to a page with three inputs.

m2-l3.title: Practice with strings, numbers, arrays, and objects
m2-l3.summary: Solve six reading-tracker problems (fixing type bugs, writing functions, working with arrays and objects, and copying an object safely), then convert pages into hours and minutes.

m3-l1.title: Make decisions, loop over data, and change the page
m3-l1.summary: Compare values with === and choose a path with if and else, repeat work with loops and the forEach, map, and filter methods, then find, change, and create page elements from your data.
m3-l1.module: Make decisions and update the page

m3-l2.title: Build a to-do list that draws itself from an array
m3-l2.summary: Store tasks in an array of objects, draw them with createElement and a render function, tick them off with checkboxes, add new ones, and clear finished ones, keeping the page in step with the data.

m3-l3.title: Practice conditions, array methods, and DOM updates
m3-l3.summary: Six problems that move from grading logic and loop statistics to drawing inventory lists and scoreboards on a page, then a challenge to build a category filter panel with an empty state.

m4-l1.title: Listen for clicks, keys, typing, and form submits
m4-l1.summary: Attach event listeners, read the event object, react to typing with the input event, stop a form's page reload with preventDefault, write validation messages people can act on, and handle a whole list with one delegated listener.

m4-l2.title: Build a sign-up form that explains its errors
m4-l2.summary: Build a club sign-up form whose rules live in one testable function, show a clear message beside each problem field, move focus to the first problem on submit, and clear messages as soon as they're fixed.

m4-l3.title: Practice events, delegation, and validation
m4-l3.summary: Build a theme switch, keyboard shortcuts, a live password checklist, an age validator, a delegated chore list, and search as you type, then upgrade the to-do list into a real form.

m5-l1.title: Schedule code with timers and save data with localStorage
m5-l1.summary: Run code later with setTimeout, repeat it with setInterval, stop it with clearInterval, and keep data across page refreshes with localStorage and JSON.

m5-l2.title: Build a pomodoro timer that remembers where it was
m5-l2.summary: Build a 25/5 pomodoro timer with Start, Pause, and Reset that counts finished focus sessions and carries on after a page refresh.

m5-l3.title: Practice: timers, countdowns, and saved data
m5-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on setTimeout, setInterval, clearTimeout, Date.now(), and localStorage with JSON, from a liftoff countdown to an autosaving draft.

m6-l1.title: Wait for data with promises, async/await, and fetch
m6-l1.summary: See how the event loop lets a page wait without freezing, then use promises, async/await, and fetch to load JSON from a real API and handle every way it can fail.
m6-l1.module: Load data with fetch and async/await

m6-l2.title: Build a GitHub profile viewer with fetch
m6-l2.summary: Build a page that looks up any GitHub user with the real GitHub API, shows their profile and recent repositories, and handles loading, not-found, rate-limit, and offline cases.

m6-l3.title: Practice: promises, async/await, and fetch
m6-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on async code, from a countdown built with await to retrying failed requests, running requests in parallel, loading dog photos from a real API, and ignoring out-of-date results.

m7-l1.title: Keep app state in one place and handle errors on purpose
m7-l1.summary: Fix the bugs that come from storing the same fact twice by keeping one state object and one render function, then throw and catch errors deliberately, guard against messy data, and split code into modules.

m7-l2.title: Build a quiz game driven by one state object
m7-l2.summary: Build a keyboard-friendly quiz with questions stored as data, one state object, pure update functions you test in Node, a render function for every screen, a saved best score, and code split into modules.

m7-l3.title: Practice: app state, errors, and modules
m7-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on keeping state in one place, deriving values, writing update functions that refuse bad input, loading settings defensively, splitting code into modules, and showing error states with a retry.

m8-l1.title: Plan your capstone browser app
m8-l1.summary: Pick a project from five ideas at different difficulty levels (or bring your own), check it against the capstone requirements, and plan its state, screens, data source, and storage before you write any code.

m8-l2.title: Build your capstone in six milestones
m8-l2.summary: Start from a working skeleton with separate modules for state, storage, data loading, and rendering, then build your own app one milestone at a time, checking each with DevTools before moving on.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your app
m8-l3.summary: Test your app's rules automatically in Node, run a test plan that covers first visits, damaged data, slow and offline networks, keyboard use, and small screens, then polish it, write a README, present it, and score it with the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Install Git and VS Code, and make a GitHub account
m1-l1.summary: Install VS Code and Git on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook, confirm both from the terminal, and create a free GitHub account.
m1-l1.module: Get set up with Git and GitHub

m1-l2.title: Set your Git identity and connect to GitHub
m1-l2.summary: Give Git your name and a private email, set two time-saving defaults, connect to GitHub with SSH or HTTPS sign-in, and prove it works by cloning a real repository.

m1-l3.title: Stay organized, stay safe, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Set up a tidy course folder, learn VS Code's Source Control view, follow the privacy rules for public repositories, and fix the Git errors beginners hit most.

m2-l1.title: Save versions with status, add, commit, log, and diff
m2-l1.summary: Learn what a commit stores, how files move from your folder to the staging area to history, and how to read status, diff, and log output.

m2-l2.title: Give a club website a clean history from day one
m2-l2.summary: Build a small robotics club website and record it in five focused commits, using a .gitignore, diffs, separate staging, and git restore along the way.

m2-l3.title: Practice reading status, splitting commits, and undoing mistakes
m2-l3.summary: Six hands-on exercises and a challenge on status codes, commit messages, focused commits, .gitignore, untracking files, searching history, and fixing the last commit.

m3-l1.title: Work on branches, merge them, and propose changes with pull requests
m3-l1.summary: Learn what a branch really is, how to switch between branches, the difference between a fast-forward and a merge commit, how remotes work, and what a pull request adds on GitHub.
m3-l1.module: Develop with branches and pull requests

m3-l2.title: Ship an events page through your first pull request
m3-l2.summary: Put the club website on GitHub, build an events page on a branch, open a pull request, update it after a self-review, merge it, and sync your computer.

m3-l3.title: Practice branching, merging, and fixing branch mistakes
m3-l3.summary: Exercises on predicting merges, running two features at once, rescuing a commit made on main, deleting branches safely, writing PR descriptions, and updating a branch with main.

m4-l1.title: Plan work with issues and boards, and review it with care
m4-l1.summary: Write issues someone else can act on, organize them with labels and a project board, link pull requests so issues close themselves, and give and receive code review well.

m4-l2.title: Run a full issue, review, and merge cycle with a partner
m4-l2.summary: Plan a change to the club website as a labeled issue on a project board, build it on a branch, get a real review with a suggested change, respond to feedback, and merge so the issue closes itself.

m4-l3.title: Practice writing issues, linking pull requests, and reviewing code
m4-l3.summary: Exercises on labeling, rewriting vague issues, splitting big tasks, predicting which pull requests close issues, rewriting harsh comments, reviewing a diff against an issue, and answering feedback.

m5-l1.title: Why merge conflicts happen and how to settle them
m5-l1.summary: Find out why Git stops some merges, read conflict markers, resolve them in the terminal or VS Code, and decide when to rebase, stash, or write a decision down.

m5-l2.title: Settle a settings conflict in VS Code and record the decision
m5-l2.summary: Build a small Quiz Night repo, create a real conflict between two teammates' settings, resolve it in VS Code's merge editor so both intentions survive, and document the choice.

m5-l3.title: Practice: conflicts, aborts, stashes, and rebases
m5-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on reading conflict markers, backing out safely, stashing new files, resolving a conflict mid-rebase, handling a deleted file, and writing a decision record.

m6-l1.title: Choose a license and give your versions meaning
m6-l1.summary: Learn what happens when a repo has no license, compare MIT, Apache-2.0, GPL-3.0, and Creative Commons in plain words, and number releases with semantic versioning and Git tags.

m6-l2.title: Ship Quiz Night 1.0.0 with a license, changelog, and tag
m6-l2.summary: Add an MIT license, turn the CHANGELOG's Unreleased section into version 1.0.0, tag it, publish a GitHub Release, then ship a 1.1.0 feature release the same way.

m6-l3.title: Practice: version numbers, licenses, changelogs, and tags
m6-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on choosing the next version, writing a version-bumping function, sorting tags, matching licenses to goals, turning a log into a changelog, and fixing a misplaced tag.

m7-l1.title: Let GitHub check every pull request, and contribute safely
m7-l1.summary: Learn how a GitHub Actions workflow runs tests on every push and pull request, how branch protection makes passing checks a rule, how forks and upstream work, and how to keep secrets out of Git.

m7-l2.title: Add a test workflow to Quiz Night and protect main
m7-l2.summary: Write a small Python module and its tests, ignore secrets with .gitignore, add a GitHub Actions workflow, watch a pull request go red and green, and require the check before merging.

m7-l3.title: Practice: workflows, forks, and keeping secrets secret
m7-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on reading triggers, fixing a broken workflow, testing on several Python versions, setting up fork remotes, reading keys from the environment, responding to a leak, and writing a CONTRIBUTING guide.

m8-l1.title: Plan a safe open-source contribution
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, pick a project at your level, learn the safety rules for working in public, and fill in a plan that takes one change from issue to merged pull request.

m8-l2.title: Build your contribution in milestones
m8-l2.summary: Work through the capstone one milestone at a time with a starter kit, a full worked example from claimed issue to synced and reviewed pull request, and fixes for the problems contributors hit most.

m8-l3.title: Check, present, and keep contributing
m8-l3.summary: Run a final test plan on your contribution, polish the pull request, present the story of your change in three minutes, write a reflection, see how it's graded, and choose what to contribute next.

m1-l1.title: Set up MakeCode and meet the micro:bit
m1-l1.summary: Open the free MakeCode editor in your browser, learn what each part of the micro:bit does, and decide whether you'll work in the simulator alone or add a real board.
m1-l1.module: Get set up with MakeCode and the micro:bit

m1-l2.title: Run your first program in the simulator and on a micro:bit
m1-l2.summary: Build a beating-heart program with a button that plays a note, test it in the simulator, then send it to a real micro:bit over USB or by copying a file.

m1-l3.title: Save your work, stay safe with hardware, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Keep MakeCode projects from disappearing, handle the board, cable, and batteries safely, set up the editor so it works for you, and follow a routine for fixing programs that misbehave.

m2-l1.title: Inputs, outputs, and the events that connect them
m2-l1.summary: Learn how on start, forever, and button events share the micro:bit, why a button press can be missed or show up late, and when to wait for an event instead of checking a button.

m2-l2.title: Build a wearable name badge that responds to buttons
m2-l2.summary: Build a badge that scrolls your name, switches between name, mood, and interest screens with button A, dims with button B, and reacts the instant you press instead of seconds later.

m2-l3.title: Practice with buttons, icons, sound, and the forever loop
m2-l3.summary: Solve six short micro:bit problems that combine button events, button checks, icons, sound, and timing, then build a secret-knock lock as a challenge.

m3-l1.title: Draw on the 5×5 LED grid and keep score with variables
m3-l1.summary: Address any LED by its x and y coordinates, move a dot with buttons, keep values in variables, add randomness, and use the touch logo and pins as extra inputs.

m3-l2.title: Build a fair reaction-time game
m3-l2.summary: Build a pocket game that waits a random time, flashes the screen, and measures how fast you press A in milliseconds, with false-start detection and a best-time record.

m3-l3.title: Practice drawing, moving, and scoring on the LED grid
m3-l3.summary: Work through six problems on plotting with loops, wrap-around movement, scorekeeping, level meters, dice faces, and filling the grid in order, then build a two-player reaction duel.

m4-l1.title: Read the accelerometer, compass, light, temperature, and microphone
m4-l1.summary: Learn what each micro:bit sensor measures and in what units, react to gestures like shake and tilt, calibrate the compass, and make steady decisions from readings that never sit perfectly still.

m4-l2.title: Build a step counter with a north-pointing compass
m4-l2.summary: Turn noisy accelerometer readings into a reliable step count with a threshold and a reset margin, test the rule on data before flashing it, and add a compass mode whose arrow always points north.

m4-l3.title: Practice with motion, light, temperature, and sound sensors
m4-l3.summary: Solve six sensor problems, from shake dice and a flicker-free night light to a spirit level, a clap counter, and an eight-point compass, then smooth a jittery light reading as a challenge.

m5-l1.title: Send radio messages between micro:bits
m5-l1.summary: Make micro:bits talk by radio with groups and the three message types, then read the same program in Blocks, JavaScript, and MicroPython.

m5-l2.title: Build a two-badge mood messenger
m5-l2.summary: Build a pair of radio badges that send moods, confirm delivery with a receipt, and warn when no reply comes, then port the finished program to MicroPython.

m5-l3.title: Practice: radio messages in MakeCode and MicroPython
m5-l3.summary: Six radio exercises, from a doorbell to a signal-strength finder, plus translating MakeCode to MicroPython and a rock-paper-scissors challenge.

m6-l1.title: React to events instead of waiting in line
m6-l1.summary: See why polling code misses button presses, switch to event handlers, keep track of what the device is doing with states, and measure time without freezing.

m6-l2.title: Build a countdown timer that never misses a press
m6-l2.summary: Build a kitchen-style countdown timer with four states, pause and resume, an alarm, and shake-to-cancel, using events and control.millis() so no press is ever lost.

m6-l3.title: Practice: event-driven devices and state games
m6-l3.summary: Rewrite polling code as events, build a lamp, a stopwatch, and an alarm with states, fix a pause that breaks a state machine, and make two state-based games.

m7-l1.title: Log sensor data and read it as a CSV
m7-l1.summary: Plan a sensor log, record it with the MakeCode data logger, get the CSV off the micro:bit, and chart it in Python to find the pattern a single reading can't show.

m7-l2.title: Build a radio sensor network with a logging hub
m7-l2.summary: Build one program that turns micro:bits into numbered sensor stations or a hub, stream every reading to the computer and the data log, warn when stations go quiet, and analyse a three-station log in Python.

m7-l3.title: Practice: collect, clean, and chart sensor data
m7-l3.summary: Plan sample rates, build a traffic-survey logger, then summarise, clean, chart, and count real-looking micro:bit logs in Python, finishing with a step counter that ignores bounces.

m8-l1.title: Plan a connected micro:bit invention
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, choose one of six project ideas, and plan its roles, radio messages, states, data, safety, and milestones before writing any code.

m8-l2.title: Build a classroom voting network in milestones
m8-l2.summary: Build the capstone's worked example, a teacher-and-voters polling network with receipts, retries, duplicate protection, and logged results, one tested milestone at a time.

m8-l3.title: Test, document, and present your invention
m8-l3.summary: Write and run a test plan, measure radio reliability with a chart, debug silent boards with a checklist, then document, present, and assess your network against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Set up Wokwi and tour the Arduino Uno
m1-l1.summary: Open a free Arduino Uno simulator in your browser, learn where everything lives in the editor and on the board, and fix the setup problems beginners usually hit.
m1-l1.module: Set up your free electronics lab

m1-l2.title: Blink an LED and print to the Serial Monitor
m1-l2.summary: Write your first Arduino sketch, blink the built-in LED, make the board print a counter to the Serial Monitor, and fix the three compile errors everyone meets first.

m1-l3.title: Work safely, save your projects, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Learn the safety rules for every circuit in the course, save Wokwi projects with or without an account, keep your work private, and follow a step-by-step routine when a circuit misbehaves.

m2-l1.title: Voltage, current, resistance, and why an LED needs a resistor
m2-l1.summary: Build an intuition for voltage, current, and resistance, use Ohm's law and the power formula to predict what a circuit will do, and see why a short circuit or a bare LED draws far too much current.

m2-l2.title: Size a resistor and light an external LED
m2-l2.summary: Calculate the right resistor for an LED, check it against the pin's current limit and the resistor's power rating, wire it in Wokwi, then fade it with PWM and add a second LED with its own resistor.

m2-l3.title: Practice: Ohm's law, power, and safe LED circuits
m2-l3.summary: Solve six circuit problems, from quick Ohm's law predictions to resistor power checks, series and parallel combinations, spotting short circuits, and estimating battery life, then write a tested circuit checker.

m3-l1.title: How breadboards connect parts, and how to read a schematic
m3-l1.summary: See which breadboard holes are joined inside, think of circuits as nodes instead of holes, read resistor color codes, wire buttons and potentiometers correctly, and turn a schematic into a breadboard layout.
m3-l1.module: Lay out breadboards and basic components

m3-l2.title: Build a button-and-knob LED controller
m3-l2.summary: Lay out a pushbutton, a potentiometer, and an LED, read the button with INPUT_PULLUP and the knob with analogRead, and combine them so the LED glows at the knob's brightness while the button is held.

m3-l3.title: Practice: breadboard faults, schematics, and button logic
m3-l3.summary: Find bypassed parts on a breadboard, decode and encode resistor colors, turn a schematic into a layout, fix miswired buttons, count presses, and remove button bounce with a millis() timer.

m4-l1.title: Digital and analog signals, and what analogRead really measures
m4-l1.summary: Learn how the Uno decides HIGH or LOW, how analogRead turns a voltage into a number from 0 to 1023, how a voltage divider lets light and temperature sensors produce that voltage, and how to smooth noisy readings.

m4-l2.title: Build a greenhouse monitor with light and temperature sensors
m4-l2.summary: Wire a light sensor and a temperature sensor in Wokwi, convert their raw readings to volts and degrees, smooth them, and switch a grow light and a fan indicator on thresholds, with all timing done by millis().

m4-l3.title: Practice: convert, smooth, and calibrate sensor readings
m4-l3.summary: Classify sensors as digital or analog, convert ADC readings without integer bugs, read a TMP36, design a voltage divider for the widest range, compare two smoothing methods, report light levels on change, and auto-calibrate a sensor.

m5-l1.title: Why motors need drivers, and how PWM sets their speed
m5-l1.summary: Compare DC motors and servos, see why an H-bridge driver and a separate battery sit between the Arduino and the wheels, and control speed with PWM.

m5-l2.title: Build a motor test bench with a speed ramp and a stop button
m5-l2.summary: Wire a knob, a stop button, a servo gauge, and three driver-input LEDs in Wokwi, then write code that ramps a motor's speed and direction safely.

m5-l3.title: Practice: motor drivers, power budgets, and servo limits
m5-l3.summary: Predict H-bridge behavior, size a battery for a robot, find wiring faults, and write motor and servo code that respects the hardware's limits.

m6-l1.title: State machines, millis() timing, and feedback loops
m6-l1.summary: Stop a robot from twitching by giving it states, timers that never block, two thresholds instead of one, and a proportional controller that steers in proportion to the error.

m6-l2.title: Build an automatic door that never closes on anyone
m6-l2.summary: Combine an ultrasonic sensor, a servo, millis() timers, and a four-state machine into a sliding-door controller with a hold-open timer and a safety reversal.

m6-l3.title: Practice: timers, state bugs, hysteresis, and tuning a P controller
m6-l3.summary: Write non-blocking timers and a servo sweep, repair a broken state machine, add hysteresis, tune a line follower's gain, and design a lost-line recovery state.

m7-l1.title: Test plans, Serial logs, calibration, and failure modes
m7-l1.summary: Design tests that vary one thing at a time, make the robot log what it's thinking, calibrate sensors against known values, and plan for the ways robots really fail.

m7-l2.title: Build a sensor test harness with fault injection and a median filter
m7-l2.summary: Log an ultrasonic sensor as CSV, fix a rounding bug the log reveals, inject the glitches real sensors produce, and prove a median filter survives them.

m7-l3.title: Practice: sensor math, test plans, log analysis, and stuck detection
m7-l3.summary: Work the ultrasonic timing math, correct for temperature, write a line-follower test plan, mine logs for flip-flops, calibrate mismatched sensors, and catch a robot that's stuck.

m8-l1.title: Plan your capstone robot before you wire anything
m8-l1.summary: Pick an obstacle-avoiding or line-following robot at your level, then plan its pins, states, safety features, power, and tests on paper first.
m8-l1.module: Capstone: an obstacle-avoiding or line-following robot

m8-l2.title: Build your robot in five milestones from a starter sketch
m8-l2.summary: Start from a working skeleton with motors, a filtered sensor, a stop button, and logging, then add the self-test, the core states, scanning or line following, and the safety features one milestone at a time.

m8-l3.title: Test your robot, write the iteration report, and present it
m8-l3.summary: Run a ten-test plan with pass criteria, record evidence from the log, write up each iteration including the regressions, present a two-minute demo, and score the project against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Install Python, VS Code, and FastAPI in a virtual environment
m1-l1.summary: Install Python 3.11+, VS Code, FastAPI, and curl on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook, then run a script that confirms every piece is in place.
m1-l1.module: Get set up with Python, FastAPI, and curl

m1-l2.title: Run your first FastAPI server and talk to it
m1-l2.summary: Write a two-route FastAPI app, start it with fastapi dev, and call it from the browser, from curl, from the /docs page, and from a TestClient script.

m1-l3.title: Organize your project, read server errors, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Set up the folder layout and two-terminal habit this course uses, find the real error behind a 500, pause a request in the VS Code debugger, and save your setup so it rebuilds anywhere.

m2-l1.title: How HTTP requests and responses actually look
m2-l1.summary: Read a real request and response from GitHub's API line by line, and learn what URLs, methods, status codes, headers, and JSON bodies each tell you.

m2-l2.title: Investigate GitHub's API with curl and a response reader
m2-l2.summary: Send real requests to GitHub's public API with curl, save the responses to files, and write a Python script that reads each one's status, headers, pagination links, and JSON.

m2-l3.title: Practice: read, build, and diagnose HTTP messages
m2-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on URLs, query strings, status codes, raw requests and responses, and diagnosing broken exchanges, all checked by running real Python.

m3-l1.title: Design REST endpoints, status codes, and JSON contracts
m3-l1.summary: Turn a messy task API into a consistent one by naming resources, choosing status codes on purpose, fixing one JSON shape for data and errors, and planning for pagination and versions.

m3-l2.title: Write the notes API contract and test it against a mock
m3-l2.summary: Design every endpoint, status code, and JSON shape of a notes API before writing a server, then build a plain-Python mock and a set of example exchanges that check the contract automatically.

m3-l3.title: Practice: fix routes, pick status codes, and page through results
m3-l3.summary: Redesign a library API's routes, choose status codes for tricky cases, normalize error shapes, write envelope pagination, detect breaking changes, and see why cursors beat offsets on a busy feed.

m4-l1.title: Turn Python functions into FastAPI routes
m4-l1.summary: Use FastAPI path parameters, query parameters, Pydantic request bodies, response models, and HTTPException to build routes that check their own input and return the right status codes.

m4-l2.title: Build the notes API in FastAPI and test it with TestClient
m4-l2.summary: Implement the notes contract from Module 3 as a FastAPI app with Pydantic models, five routes, correct status codes, and an in-memory list, then call it with curl and prove it works with a unittest suite.

m4-l3.title: Practice: extend the notes API and catch bugs with tests
m4-l3.summary: Add a health check, a count route, a Location header, PUT, a 409 for duplicate titles, and a versioned paginated list to the notes API, write a test that catches a paging bug, and replay the Module 3 contract against FastAPI.

m5-l1.title: Store club data in related SQL tables
m5-l1.summary: Split a one-table sign-up sheet into members, events, and sign-ups linked by keys, then query it back with WHERE, ORDER BY, JOIN, and GROUP BY in SQLite.

m5-l2.title: Build the notes app's database in SQLite
m5-l2.summary: Design and build a four-table SQLite database for the notes API, with the queries it needs, owner-checked updates, an index, and a transaction that saves a note and its tags together.

m5-l3.title: Practice SQL on a school library database
m5-l3.summary: Write filters, joins, grouped counts, a many-to-many design, a transactional checkout, and a normalization script against a small SQLite library.

m6-l1.title: Guard the API: validation, SQL injection, passwords, and permissions
m6-l1.summary: Check each request in order (shape, identity, permission), see a real SQL injection and its fix, hash passwords with scrypt, and learn what CORS and rate limits do.

m6-l2.title: Add accounts, tokens, and owner-only notes to the API
m6-l2.summary: Extend the notes API with sign-up, login, scrypt-hashed passwords, bearer tokens, a current_user dependency, and ownership checks, then prove each rule with TestClient tests.

m6-l3.title: Practice validation, safe queries, password storage, and limits
m6-l3.summary: Tighten a Pydantic model, close two kinds of SQL injection, store PBKDF2 hashes that can be upgraded, write a role-based permission rule, rate-limit a login route, and test a CORS setup.

m7-l1.title: Connect a web page to a database-backed API, errors included
m7-l1.summary: Follow one click from fetch to FastAPI to SQLite and back, open a database connection per request with a dependency, map failures to the right status codes, and make the page show what actually went wrong.
m7-l1.module: Connect the browser, API, and database

m7-l2.title: Build the full notes app: SQLite, FastAPI, and a web page
m7-l2.summary: Move the notes API onto SQLite with a connection dependency, test it against a separate database, write a page that calls it with fetch and shows real errors, serve both from one app, and learn the free ways to put it online.

m7-l3.title: Practice wiring the layers together and reporting errors well
m7-l3.summary: Prove a connection dependency always cleans up, turn constraint failures into clear 409s, page through results, format 422 errors and token failures in JavaScript, nest related rows in JSON, and give every error one shape.

m8-l1.title: Plan a database-backed web app people could really use
m8-l1.summary: Pick a capstone project, then plan its tables, routes, JSON, validation, and permission rules on paper, and test the schema in SQLite before writing a single route.

m8-l2.title: Build the book club tracker in five milestones
m8-l2.summary: Start from a working starter with accounts and books, then add reviews, owner-only edits, logout, and a browser page, checking each milestone with TestClient before moving on.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your web app
m8-l3.summary: Turn your route table into an automated test suite on its own database, polish errors and documentation, present a three-minute demo, and score your project against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Install Unity Hub, Unity 6, and a C# code editor
m1-l1.summary: Check your computer, install Unity Hub and the Unity 6.3 LTS Editor on Windows, macOS, or Linux, connect a free C# editor, and fix the install problems that stop most people.
m1-l1.module: Set up Unity 6

m1-l2.title: Create a Universal 2D project and run your first script
m1-l2.summary: Create the course project from the Universal 2D template, learn the six Editor windows you'll use every day, and prove the whole toolchain works with a script that spins a square and answers a key press.

m1-l3.title: Save, back up, and debug your Unity projects
m1-l3.summary: Keep your work safe with scene saves, a tidy Assets folder, and Git, read the Console like a pro, and follow a routine for getting unstuck that works on any Unity error.

m2-l1.title: How Unity builds a scene from GameObjects, components, and prefabs
m2-l1.summary: Learn what GameObjects and components are, how Transforms and parenting place things, when Unity calls Awake, Start, and Update, and how prefabs keep repeated objects in sync.

m2-l2.title: Build a hazard course from one saw-blade prefab
m2-l2.summary: Build a spinning saw blade from a sprite, a child object, and a script, turn it into a prefab, place copies, change them all at once, and make a bobbing variant that inherits from the original.

m2-l3.title: Practice: components, the frame loop, and prefabs
m2-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on Transforms, GetComponent, the order Unity calls your code, spawning prefabs from scripts, timers, and planning prefab variants.

m3-l1.title: Move with C# using vectors, speed, and Time.deltaTime
m3-l1.summary: Make movement that runs at the same speed on every computer, tune it from the Inspector, read the keyboard with the Input System, keep diagonals from being faster, and flip a sprite to face where it's going.

m3-l2.title: Build a top-down explorer that moves the same on every computer
m3-l2.summary: Write a C# movement script step by step, from raw key reading to normalized diagonals, smooth acceleration, a sprint key, facing, and arena walls, testing the speed with real numbers as you go.

m3-l3.title: Practice: movement, timers, and the mouse in C#
m3-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge that fix common C# compile errors, prove frame-rate independence, and add a dash, mouse following, screen wrapping, tile-by-tile movement, and a turret that aims and fires.

m4-l1.title: Rigidbody 2D, colliders, collision events, and cameras that follow
m4-l1.summary: Hand movement to Unity's 2D physics engine with Rigidbody 2D and colliders, learn when collision and trigger events fire, keep fast objects from tunneling through walls, filter with layers, and plan a follow camera that's comfortable to watch.

m4-l2.title: Build a jumping player with a ground check and a Cinemachine camera
m4-l2.summary: Turn the hazard course into a playable platformer with a Rigidbody 2D player that runs, jumps only when grounded, respawns when a saw hits it, collects coins, and is followed by a damped, bounded Cinemachine camera.

m4-l3.title: Practice: better jumps, triggers, layers, and camera zones
m4-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge that add a kill zone, variable jump height, coyote time, a jump buffer, a tunneling test, layer-filtered crates, and a Cinemachine zoom zone to the platformer.

m5-l1.title: Make the game talk back with Animator states, a HUD, and sound
m5-l1.summary: Drive sprite animations from code with Animator parameters and transitions, show score and health with TextMeshPro on a scaled Canvas, and layer sound effects with AudioSource.
m5-l1.module: Feedback with animation, UI, and audio

m5-l2.title: Build a HUD with a score, a health bar, hurt feedback, and sound
m5-l2.summary: Add coins that raise a TextMeshPro score, spikes that drain a slider health bar, a flashing hurt animation with sound, and a game-over panel with a working Restart button.

m5-l3.title: Practice: falling animations, timers, footsteps, and a pause menu
m5-l3.summary: Add a Fall state, fix an ambiguous Random error, build a countdown timer, footstep and heartbeat sounds, and a pause menu that freezes the game without freezing the UI.

m6-l1.title: Enemies as state machines, and levels that teach before they test
m6-l1.summary: Model enemy behavior as Patrol, Chase, and Search states with waypoints and line of sight, spawn enemies from prefabs on a timer, tune difficulty with a few numbers, and lay out levels that introduce one idea at a time.

m6-l2.title: Build a level slice with a tilemap, a sentry drone, and a spawner
m6-l2.summary: Paint a level on Tilemaps with merged colliders, build a drone that patrols waypoints, chases on sight, and searches where it lost you, then add a capped spawner and arrange the slice to teach, test, and twist.

m6-l3.title: Practice: patrol routes, ledge walkers, telegraphed attacks, and waves
m6-l3.summary: Write a ping-pong patrol and a ground enemy that turns at ledges, repair a level that tests before it teaches, add a wind-up attack, check spawn pacing with numbers, and build a wave spawner.

m7-l1.title: Save progress, playtest, profile, and make a build that behaves like the Editor
m7-l1.summary: Choose between PlayerPrefs and JSON save files, write and read a save with JsonUtility and Application.persistentDataPath, run a useful playtest, read the Profiler, and set up a Web build in Unity 6 Build Profiles.

m7-l2.title: Save at checkpoints, then publish a Web build on itch.io
m7-l2.summary: Write a save system that uses a JSON file on desktop and PlayerPrefs on the Web, save at checkpoints and restore on load, keep a volume setting, then make a Web build with Build Profiles and publish it free on itch.io.

m7-l3.title: Practice: high scores, save bugs, collected coins, profiling, and playtest data
m7-l3.summary: Keep a best score, find why a save silently drops data, remember which coins were collected, upgrade old save files, fix a script the Profiler flags, and turn a playtest log into a decision.

m8-l1.title: Plan your capstone game, from a one-line pitch to four milestones
m8-l1.summary: Pick one of five project ideas (or your own), cut it to a size you can finish, write a one-page game design document, plan four milestones, and line up art and sound you're allowed to use.
m8-l1.module: Capstone: a complete game of your own

m8-l2.title: Build your capstone in four milestones, starting from a game skeleton
m8-l2.summary: Set up a title screen, levels, and an end screen with a GameManager state machine, then build through grey box, vertical slice, content complete, and ship, with a bug list and a feature freeze.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your game, then keep going
m8-l3.summary: Run a written test plan in the Editor and the Web build, playtest a second round, polish in order of impact, capture screenshots and a short trailer, build the itch.io page, present a three-minute demo, and score the project against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Open Google Colab and run your first notebook
m1-l1.summary: Sign in to Google Colab, create a notebook, run Python cells, and confirm that pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib are ready, with JupyterLab as the local option.
m1-l1.module: Set up your data notebook

m1-l2.title: Upload a CSV, chart it, and save your results to Drive
m1-l2.summary: Tour the Colab window, get a CSV file from your computer into the runtime, load and chart it with pandas, and keep the results safe in Google Drive.

m1-l3.title: Keep notebooks reproducible, organized, and easy to debug
m1-l3.summary: Avoid hidden-state bugs, test a notebook with a clean restart, lay notebooks out so they read top to bottom, and get unstuck when pandas throws an error.

m2-l1.title: Load CSV and JSON files and check what pandas actually sees
m2-l1.summary: Read CSV and JSON exports into pandas, run a first-look checklist (shape, head, dtypes, info, describe), and spot the one bad value that turns a number column into text.
m2-l1.module: Load and inspect CSV and JSON data

m2-l2.title: Build a first-look report for messy survey exports
m2-l2.summary: Load the same commute survey from a CSV form export and a JSON app export, write a reusable first_look() report that flags text hiding in number columns, and chart where the two exports disagree.

m2-l3.title: Practice: load and inspect six tricky data files
m2-l3.summary: Load CSV and JSON files that break in the classic ways (semicolons, lost leading zeros, nested lists, text in number columns) and inspect each one until you know what pandas really loaded.

m3-l1.title: Compute on whole columns with NumPy arrays and pandas DataFrames
m3-l1.summary: Replace slow Python loops with vectorized NumPy math, pick rows with boolean masks, select with loc and iloc, add columns, and summarize and join tables with groupby and merge.

m3-l2.title: Build a bike-share station report with groupby and merge
m3-l2.summary: Turn 5,000 raw bike-share trips into a station report by computing trip times with vectorized date math, adding columns, summarizing with groupby, and joining station details with merge.

m3-l3.title: Practice: vectorize, filter, group, and join tables
m3-l3.summary: Rewrite loops as array math, answer questions with boolean masks, select with loc and iloc, build columns, summarize with groupby, and find unmatched rows in a merge.

m4-l1.title: Find and fix missing, duplicate, wrong, and impossible values
m4-l1.summary: Repair the classic problems in a messy sensor log (text in number columns, disguised missing values, duplicates, inconsistent category names, impossible readings) and learn when an outlier should stay.

m4-l2.title: Clean a messy street-tree survey step by step
m4-l2.summary: Take a volunteer tree survey with mixed units, misspelled species, disguised missing values, re-surveyed trees, and impossible heights, clean it one logged step at a time, and see how cleaning changes the answer.
