m4-l3.title: Practice: clean six small messes, then a whole dataset
m4-l3.summary: Fix disguised missing values, near-duplicate sign-ups, prices stored as text, inconsistent sizes, suspicious reaction times, and a wide gradebook, then write a cleaning function for an animal-shelter log.

m5-l1.title: Describe a distribution with center, spread, and the right chart
m5-l1.summary: Compare means and medians, measure spread with standard deviation and IQR, read histograms and box plots, and pick a bar, line, scatter, or distribution chart to fit the question.

m5-l2.title: Rebuild a misleading chart so it tells the truth
m5-l2.summary: Take apart a newsletter's truncated bar chart and dual-axis line chart, measure how much they exaggerate, and rebuild them with honest axes, every data point visible, consistent colors, and titles that state the finding.

m5-l3.title: Practice: summaries, distributions, and honest charts
m5-l3.summary: Choose between mean and median, read histograms and box plots, match questions to chart types, fix a truncated bar chart and a color-only chart, and meet four datasets with identical statistics.

m6-l1.title: Correlation, confounders, and samples that mislead
m6-l1.summary: Measure correlation with r, see how a hidden common cause creates a convincing pattern, show how a biased sample stays wrong however large it gets, spot survivorship bias, and write claims that stay within what the data shows.
m6-l1.module: Test claims for confounders and bias

m6-l2.title: Untangle Simpson's paradox in the 1973 Berkeley admissions
m6-l2.summary: Rebuild the real UC Berkeley graduate admissions numbers for six departments, find out why men's overall admission rate was higher even though women did as well or better in most departments, and write a claim the data can support.

m6-l3.title: Practice: confounders, biased samples, and reversals
m6-l3.summary: Find the strongest correlation in a survey, uncover a confounder that makes tutoring look harmful, reweight a lopsided survey, measure survivorship bias, analyze real kidney stone data, rewrite overconfident claims, and build your own Simpson's paradox.

m7-l1.title: Make a notebook anyone can rerun and get the same answer
m7-l1.summary: Avoid hidden state, make cells safe to rerun, fix randomness with seeds, check your work with Restart session and run all, and guard your data with assertions so a notebook reproduces its results for anyone.

m7-l2.title: Build a bus-delay report that rebuilds itself from raw data
m7-l2.summary: Turn a raw CSV of school bus arrivals into a rerunnable report with a parameters cell, a cleaning log, assertions, three purpose-built charts, a one-figure dashboard, exported images, and an executive summary written from computed numbers.

m7-l3.title: Practice: rerunnable notebooks and summaries that can't go stale
m7-l3.summary: Make random results repeatable, find and fix hidden state, replace hand-typed numbers with computed ones, write data checks, name and title exported figures, generate an executive summary, and measure how much a result moves between seeds.

m8-l1.title: Plan a reproducible data investigation
m8-l1.summary: Choose a capstone project at the right difficulty, turn a vague interest into a question your data can answer, run a 15-minute first look to check the data is up to it, and fill in a plan covering charts, bias, and milestones.

m8-l2.title: Build your investigation milestone by milestone
m8-l2.summary: Start from a Colab notebook skeleton, then follow a complete worked example (BMI and diabetes progression in 442 patients) through loading, documenting, cleaning, summarizing, checking for confounders, building a dashboard, and writing an executive summary with limits.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your investigation
m8-l3.summary: Put your capstone through six tests (fresh run, someone else's run, tampered data, changed seeds and cutoffs, and overclaiming words), polish your charts, present the findings in five minutes, and score your work against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Open Teachable Machine and let it use your camera
m1-l1.summary: Open Google's free Teachable Machine in your browser, find your way around its three panels, give it camera access, and learn exactly where your pictures go.
m1-l1.module: Get set up with Teachable Machine

m1-l2.title: Train your first model to tell thumbs up from thumbs down
m1-l2.summary: Record two classes of webcam examples, train a model in about a minute, and prove it works by testing it on things it has never seen, including an empty room.

m1-l3.title: Save your projects, keep a model journal, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Save Teachable Machine projects so a closed tab never costs you an hour, record every experiment in a one-page journal, fix the common problems fast, and optionally open Google Colab.

m2-l1.title: Rules, machine learning, and AI, and the five kinds of tasks
m2-l1.summary: Tell a hand-written rule from a learned model, place AI, machine learning, and deep learning inside each other, and name the task a system does by the shape of its answer.

m2-l2.title: Build a clap detector, then try to beat it with a rule
m2-l2.summary: Write a simple loudness rule for spotting claps, train a Teachable Machine sound model to tell claps, snaps, and silence apart, and test both to see where each one breaks.

m2-l3.title: Practice: rules or learning, which task, and what a chatbot can't promise
m2-l3.summary: Sort real systems into rules or learned models, name their task families, reframe one goal four ways, and judge claims people make about chatbots.

m3-l1.title: Features, labels, and examples, the way a model sees them
m3-l1.summary: Describe any dataset as a table of examples, features, and a label, see how the features you pick decide what a model can tell apart, and separate training from making predictions.
m3-l1.module: Describe examples with features and labels

m3-l2.title: Train a recycling sorter and watch your examples shape it
m3-l2.summary: Build a Teachable Machine image model that sorts paper from plastic, break it with a narrow set of examples, fix it by changing only the examples, and catch it learning a shortcut.

m3-l3.title: Practice: build the table, choose the label, and predict what the model learns
m3-l3.summary: Turn real situations into examples, features, and labels, catch features that leak the answer, write labeling rules, read a decision boundary, and predict the shortcuts a model will take.

m4-l1.title: Test on examples the model never saw, and see how a network learns
m4-l1.summary: Split data into training, validation, and test sets, recognize overfitting from training and test error, and follow how a neural network nudges its weights to make fewer mistakes.
m4-l1.module: Test models fairly and see how networks learn

m4-l2.title: Train a neural network you can see inside, then make it overfit
m4-l2.summary: Use TensorFlow Playground to train a small neural network in your browser, watch its neurons and weights change, push it into overfitting on purpose, and fix it three different ways.

m4-l3.title: Practice: spot the leak, read the curves, and nudge a neuron
m4-l3.summary: Find test sets that aren't really new, diagnose models from their training and test curves, split data by person, work a neuron by hand, and predict what learning rates and epochs will do.

m5-l1.title: Confidence scores, thresholds, and who pays for the mistakes
m5-l1.summary: Learn what a confidence score really measures, how a threshold trades false positives for false negatives, and how the Gender Shades study exposed errors that an overall accuracy number hid.
m5-l1.module: Read confidence and check for bias

m5-l2.title: Stress-test a rock-paper-scissors model and chart where it fails
m5-l2.summary: Train a four-class gesture model, test it 36 times in conditions it never saw, then turn your log into a confusion matrix, accuracy by condition, and a "not sure" threshold.

m5-l3.title: Practice: read scores, set thresholds, and find who the errors land on
m5-l3.summary: Six judgement problems on confidence, false positives and negatives, thresholds, a rare-disease puzzle, accuracy by group, and where bias comes from, plus a fairness test plan of your own.

m6-l1.title: What models remember, and why "anonymous" data often isn't
m6-l1.summary: See how models can memorize training data, why removing names rarely makes data anonymous, what real consent looks like, why face recognition is so disputed, and what COPPA requires for kids under 13.

m6-l2.title: Write a data and consent plan before you record anyone
m6-l2.summary: Take a club's plan to collect faces and voices "in case they're useful," and turn it into a one-page data plan with a clear purpose, the least data that works, a consent form, and a deletion date.

m6-l3.title: Practice: spot privacy risks, fix consent, and test whether data is anonymous
m6-l3.summary: Six privacy problems, from sorting personal data and rewriting a bad consent form to testing a survey table for anonymity, checking apps against COPPA, and debating face recognition at a school entrance.

m7-l1.title: Deepfakes, chatbot hallucinations, and when AI is the wrong tool
m7-l1.summary: Learn why chatbots state false things fluently, how real deepfakes have fooled people, a four-step method for checking media, and five questions that decide whether AI fits a problem at all.
m7-l1.module: Check AI-made media and decide if AI fits

m7-l2.title: Fact-check a chatbot answer, one claim at a time
m7-l2.summary: Take a confident chatbot-style answer about the Gender Shades study, split it into nine checkable claims, trace each one to the original paper, and rewrite it so every sentence is true.

m7-l3.title: Practice: check viral claims and judge whether AI fits
m7-l3.summary: Six problems on spotting risky claims, checking a viral post, planning against voice-clone scams, ranking chatbot tasks by risk, doing the math on an AI essay detector, and scoring three real-style AI proposals.

m8-l1.title: Pick a real problem and plan your AI recommendation
m8-l1.summary: Choose one of five proposals (or your own), map everyone it would affect, plan the evidence you'll gather, and fill in a one-page plan for a recommendation on whether and how AI should be used.
m8-l1.module: Capstone: should AI do this job?

m8-l2.title: Build your recommendation in six milestones
m8-l2.summary: Fill in a memo template one milestone at a time (problem, data, prototype evidence, risks, alternatives, verdict), following a worked example whose evidence ends up changing its own verdict.

m8-l3.title: Test, present, and grade your AI recommendation
m8-l3.summary: Stress-test your memo the way you stress-tested a model (fact-check, red team, affected-person read), present it in three minutes, grade it against the rubric, and choose what to learn next.

m1-l1.title: What you need to train a model in your browser
m1-l1.summary: Check your computer, browser, and webcam, give Teachable Machine permission to use the camera, and learn exactly where your photos and recordings go.
m1-l1.module: Get set up with Teachable Machine

m1-l2.title: Train your first model in five minutes
m1-l2.summary: Open an Image Project, record two classes from your webcam, click Train Model, and watch the preview bars respond to your hand.

m1-l3.title: Save your projects, record people fairly, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Save a project as a file or to Google Drive and reopen it, keep a project log, follow the course's consent rules for recording people, and fix the problems that stop beginners.

m2-l1.title: Choose classes a model can tell apart, and examples that cover the world
m2-l1.summary: Define classes that a single camera frame can separate, decide how many examples each needs, vary lighting, angle, distance, and background on purpose, and record only people who agreed.

m2-l2.title: Collect a rock, paper, scissors dataset you can trust
m2-l2.summary: Plan four classes, record Rock, Paper, Scissors, and Nothing in rotating sessions across lighting, distance, and both hands, clean out bad frames, and save version 1 with a project log.

m2-l3.title: Practice: design classes and stress-test your data
m2-l3.summary: Fix overlapping class lists, then run hands-on Teachable Machine experiments that show what happens with no Nothing class, a background shortcut, too few samples, and a pose recorded in one spot.

m3-l1.title: Why lopsided data makes a lopsided model, and what Train Model does
m3-l1.summary: See why a class with ten times more examples takes over a model's answers, then learn what epochs, batch size, and learning rate control, and how to read the accuracy and loss graphs under the hood.
m3-l1.module: Balance data and train in the browser

m3-l2.title: Balance and train your rock, paper, scissors model
m3-l2.summary: Train your version 1 dataset with the graphs open, read per-class accuracy and the confusion matrix, watch a lopsided copy go wrong, then make one targeted, balanced fix and save version 2.

m3-l3.title: Practice: imbalance, epochs, and learning rate experiments
m3-l3.summary: Work out what lopsided counts do to accuracy, count batches and adjustments, read three sets of learning curves, and run hands-on experiments with epochs, learning rate, and rebalancing in Teachable Machine.

m4-l1.title: What the confidence bars mean, and why 99% can still be wrong
m4-l1.summary: Learn where Teachable Machine's percentages come from, why a model can be confidently wrong on things it has never seen, and how to plan tests with new people, places, and lighting.
m4-l1.module: Interpret confidence and test on unseen examples

m4-l2.title: Build an unseen test set and run your model against it
m4-l2.summary: Plan and photograph 40 test images in places, light, and hands your model has never seen, run each through the preview, record the answer and its confidence on a test sheet, and compare the result with a familiar test.

m4-l3.title: Practice: read confidence and test a recycling sorter on new objects
m4-l3.summary: Read and predict confidence bars, build a quick recycling sorter with held-out items, test it on new objects, surfaces, and things it has no class for, and choose a confidence threshold from test results.

m5-l1.title: Read a confusion matrix and tell false positives from false negatives
m5-l1.summary: Turn test results into a confusion matrix, find the exact pair of classes your model mixes up, and decide which kind of mistake matters more for your app.

m5-l2.title: Fix the Scissors-Paper mix-up with targeted examples
m5-l2.summary: Test your rock, paper, scissors model on unseen photos, build its confusion matrix, trace the worst mistake to a gap in the training data, fill that gap, and retest on the same photos.

m5-l3.title: Practice: diagnose errors in doorbells, sorters, and sign helpers
m5-l3.summary: Count false positives and negatives, spot which classes a model confuses, match errors to their causes, judge whether a data change really helped, and catch a retest that cheats.

m6-l1.title: Export a model, and know what you're giving away
m6-l1.summary: Learn what each Teachable Machine export option produces and where it runs, what a shared link or downloaded file reveals about you and the people in your data, and what a model card adds that the file can't say.

m6-l2.title: Publish your rock, paper, scissors model with a model card
m6-l2.summary: Run a pre-export check, upload your model for a shareable link, download a backup, and write a one-page model card whose numbers come straight from your unseen test.

m6-l3.title: Practice: choose exports, audit labels, and write model cards
m6-l3.summary: Pick the right export for each device, find what a model's files give away, fix weak model cards, and decide which models are safe to share.

m7-l1.title: Make an app act on predictions without the jitter
m7-l1.summary: See how exported Teachable Machine code turns camera frames into scores, find the three lines you actually change, and calm a jumpy model with a confidence threshold, a hold time, and a cooldown.

m7-l2.title: Play rock, paper, scissors against the computer with your webcam
m7-l2.summary: Load your model into a p5.js sketch with ml5.js, lock in a move only when it's held steadily for a second, play against a random computer opponent, and re-arm the game with the Nothing class.

m7-l3.title: Practice: doorbells, posture reminders, and a sign-language letter helper
m7-l3.summary: Write the rules between a model's label and an app's action for audio, pose, and image projects, test each one on recorded predictions, and pick a threshold from real logged scores.

m8-l1.title: Plan your interactive ML prototype
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, pick one of five project ideas (or your own), and fill in a one-page plan covering classes, consent, data, unseen tests, the error that matters most, and the rule that turns predictions into actions.
m8-l1.module: Capstone: build an interactive ML prototype

m8-l2.title: Build your prototype milestone by milestone
m8-l2.summary: Work through data, testing, one repair round, export, and the app in order, using a starter sketch that turns any image or sound model into an app through a settings block and an actions table.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your prototype
m8-l3.summary: Stress-test your prototype in the conditions it will really meet, polish what users see, add a keyboard fallback, present a three-minute demo that includes an explained failure, and check your work against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Get a free Colab notebook ready for machine learning
m1-l1.summary: Open Google Colab in your browser, create a notebook in your Drive, learn the keys you'll press every lesson, and run a check that proves scikit-learn, pandas, and matplotlib are ready.
m1-l1.module: Set up Colab and scikit-learn

m1-l2.title: Train your first model in five lines
m1-l2.summary: Load 150 measured iris flowers, train a k-nearest-neighbors model in five lines of scikit-learn, and check its guesses on flowers it has never seen.

m1-l3.title: Keep notebooks safe, tidy, and fixable
m1-l3.summary: Find and back up your notebooks in Google Drive, lay them out so they run top to bottom after a restart, and use a five-step routine to fix scikit-learn errors.

m2-l1.title: Features, targets, and the fit-predict pattern
m2-l1.summary: Follow the machine-learning workflow from question to prediction, turn a table into a feature table X and a target y, and decide which columns a model is allowed to use.
m2-l1.module: Features, targets, and the ML workflow

m2-l2.title: Build a pizza delivery-time predictor
m2-l2.summary: Write a column plan for a 300-order log, build X and y from it, train a model, measure its error in minutes against a do-nothing baseline, and catch two leaky columns before they fool you.

m2-l3.title: Practice choosing features and targets
m2-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on shaping data for scikit-learn, from reading a picture as a row of numbers to hunting down a leaky column by its suspiciously good score.

m3-l1.title: Hold out a test set, then scale and encode fairly
m3-l1.summary: Split data with train_test_split and stratify, learn why the test set must stay untouched, and prepare features with StandardScaler and one-hot encoding without leaking test information into training.

m3-l2.title: Prepare game-player data so k-NN can use it
m3-l2.summary: Take a table of new players with wildly different units and a text column, split it with stratify, scale and one-hot encode it without leaks, and watch k-NN go from worse than guessing to over 90% accurate.

m3-l3.title: Practice splitting, scaling, and encoding
m3-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on honest data preparation, from the sorted-data trap and stratified splits to scaling by hand, fixing leaky code, and building a pipeline for used-bike listings.

m4-l1.title: Predict from nearby examples or from a straight line
m4-l1.summary: Learn how k-nearest neighbors classifies by letting the closest examples vote, how k reshapes its decision boundary, and how linear regression fits a line by shrinking its residuals, with a first look at gradient descent.

m4-l2.title: Write gradient descent yourself, then race a line against k-NN
m4-l2.summary: Code a gradient descent line-fitter from scratch for the diabetes data, check that it lands on the same line as scikit-learn, then compare linear regression and k-NN regression on unseen patients.

m4-l3.title: Practice with neighbors, lines, and learning rates
m4-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on k-NN and linear regression, from voting by hand and choosing k with a validation set to residuals, learning rates that blow up, and writing k-NN from scratch.

m5-l1.title: Probabilities from logistic regression, rules from decision trees
m5-l1.summary: Squash a score into a probability with the sigmoid, choose a decision threshold, and read the yes-or-no questions a decision tree learns, including how Gini impurity picks each split.

m5-l2.title: Build a spam filter that gives probabilities and readable rules
m5-l2.summary: Train logistic regression and a decision tree on 600 simulated messages, choose a spam threshold that protects real mail, and read the tree's rules out loud.

m5-l3.title: Practice: sigmoids, thresholds, and hand-built splits
m5-l3.summary: Write the sigmoid yourself, find a 50/50 point, turn probabilities into decisions, compute Gini impurity, search for the best split by hand, and test how tree depth changes accuracy.

m6-l1.title: Accuracy, confusion matrices, and metrics that fit the job
m6-l1.summary: See why accuracy misleads when the thing you're hunting is rare, split predictions into a confusion matrix, measure precision, recall, and F1, and score number predictions with MAE, RMSE, and R².

m6-l2.title: Tune an icy-road warning with a confusion matrix and a threshold
m6-l2.summary: Build a full metrics report for a rare-event classifier, sweep the decision threshold to trade false alarms for missed ice, choose it on validation data, and confirm it once on the test set.

m6-l3.title: Practice: confusion counts, metric choices, and error sizes
m6-l3.summary: Count confusion-matrix boxes by hand, write precision, recall, and F1 yourself, match metrics to real situations, fix a wrong-positive-class bug, and score regression models with MAE, RMSE, and R².

m7-l1.title: Spot underfitting and overfitting, then compare models fairly
m7-l1.summary: Read the gap between training and validation scores, draw a validation curve over tree depth, use cross-validation to stop trusting one lucky split, and compare three models under the same rules.

m7-l2.title: Choose a model for diabetes progression with cross-validation
m7-l2.summary: Lock away a test set, tune a tree's depth and k-NN's k with cross-validated curves, compare four models on the same folds with error bars, and test the winner exactly once.

m7-l3.title: Practice: fit diagnoses, fold traps, and fair model contests
m7-l3.summary: Write a fit-diagnosis function, draw a k-NN validation curve, escape the sorted-data fold trap, measure how much one split wobbles, run a fair three-model contest, and repair a leaky tuning loop.

m8-l1.title: Plan a model comparison you can defend
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, pick one of five projects at different levels, write a data card and a plan before any modeling code, and see the milestones and rubric you'll work toward.

m8-l2.title: Build the comparison milestone by milestone
m8-l2.summary: Start from a runnable starter notebook, then grow it through seven milestones on the handwritten digits, from data card and baseline to a fit diagnosis, one test-set score, a gallery of misread digits, and a written recommendation.

m8-l3.title: Check, polish, and present your model comparison
m8-l3.summary: Add automatic checks that catch leaks and broken splits, make the notebook rerun cleanly, turn your results into a chart with a conclusion for a title, present in three minutes, and grade yourself with the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Set up a free Pico W lab in Wokwi, plus optional real hardware
m1-l1.summary: Open a simulated Raspberry Pi Pico W running MicroPython in your browser, learn the editor and the board's pins, and install the optional tools for a real Pico W or Raspberry Pi.
m1-l1.module: Set up your Pico W lab

m1-l2.title: Blink the Pico W's LED, then one you wire yourself
m1-l2.summary: Run your first MicroPython program on a simulated Pico W, wire an external LED with a resistor, control both from the REPL, and optionally do the same on a real Raspberry Pi over SSH.

m1-l3.title: Save your projects, read error messages, and work safely
m1-l3.summary: Keep your Wokwi projects safe and organized, read MicroPython tracebacks, follow a debugging routine for hardware, and learn the privacy, accessibility, and electrical safety rules this course relies on.

m2-l1.title: Use the Linux terminal and read GPIO pins without breaking anything
m2-l1.summary: Move around a Linux system with the terminal, handle files, sudo, and permissions safely, then tell GPIO numbers from physical pins and keep every connection inside the 3.3 V and current limits.
m2-l1.module: Linux basics and safe GPIO wiring

m2-l2.title: Check a wiring plan with Python before you build it
m2-l2.summary: Set up a project folder from the terminal, write a Python tool that catches wrong pins, reused pins, 5 V signals, and overloaded outputs in a wiring plan, then wire the approved plan in Wokwi and smoke-test every connection.

m2-l3.title: Practice: terminal navigation, permissions, pin maps, and safe signal levels
m2-l3.summary: Solve six problems that mix Linux and electronics, from predicting where cd lands and fixing permission errors to auditing a Raspberry Pi wiring list, sizing LED resistors for 3.3 V, and designing a voltage divider, then catch PWM pin conflicts in a challenge.

m3-l1.title: Read buttons and knobs, drive LEDs and servos, and never block the loop
m3-l1.summary: Read digital inputs with pull-ups and debouncing, turn analog voltages into numbers with the Pico W's ADC, sanity-check the onboard temperature sensor, control brightness and servo angle with PWM, and run several jobs at once with ticks_ms.

m3-l2.title: Build a status panel with a dimmer, a light alarm, and a servo gauge
m3-l2.summary: Program the Module 2 circuit plus a servo into a responsive status panel that dims an LED from a knob, blinks an alarm when it gets dark, swings a gauge needle, and switches modes on a debounced button, all in one non-blocking loop.

m3-l3.title: Practice: clean sensor readings, debounced buttons, and outputs that don't chatter
m3-l3.summary: Turn raw ADC numbers into trustworthy values with dead zones, averaging, and a thermistor formula that detects broken wiring, then count bouncy button presses, stop an alarm from chattering, survive the tick counter wrapping, and build a non-blocking vent controller.

m4-l1.title: Sample, timestamp, smooth, and package sensor data
m4-l1.summary: Choose a sampling rate without missing events or filling the flash, timestamp readings with the right clock, log them as CSV, smooth noise with moving and exponential averages, package readings as JSON, and buffer them through a network outage.
m4-l1.module: Log, smooth, and send sensor data

m4-l2.title: Build a Wi-Fi data logger that survives a network outage
m4-l2.summary: Turn a simulated Pico W into a logger that timestamps temperature and light readings with NTP, writes them to a CSV file in batches, queues them as JSON, and posts them over Wi-Fi, keeping every reading through an outage you trigger with a switch.

m4-l3.title: Practice: analyze sensor logs, find gaps, and validate payloads
m4-l3.summary: Work with real-shaped logger output in Python: estimate storage, summarize a log with sensor faults, locate missing readings, choose a smoothing strength from measured noise and lag, resample with pandas, validate JSON payloads, and merge late and duplicated deliveries.

m5-l1.title: Route readings through an MQTT broker with clear topics, QoS, and last will
m5-l1.summary: Learn how publish/subscribe works, design topic names a dashboard can understand, pick a QoS level, and use retained messages and last will so a new subscriber knows what is going on.

m5-l2.title: Publish live greenhouse readings from a Pico W and watch them on a dashboard
m5-l2.summary: Connect a simulated Pico W and DHT22 to a public MQTT broker, publish labelled JSON readings with a retained status and last will, watch them in the HiveMQ web client, and build a browser dashboard that marks stale values.

m5-l3.title: Practice: topic plans, wildcard routing, payload checks, and a chart dashboard
m5-l3.summary: Fix a messy topic scheme, validate and route wildcard subscriptions, reject bad payloads, find lost and duplicate messages, draw a stale-aware chart, and build a tiny broker with retained messages and last will.

m6-l1.title: Decide who may switch the fan with device identity, TLS, and signed commands
m6-l1.summary: Separate identity, authentication, and authorization, see what TLS protects and what it leaves open, sign commands with HMAC so only key holders can create them, and stop replayed messages with timestamps, nonces, or counters.

m6-l2.title: Build a signed fan command that rejects forgeries and replays
m6-l2.summary: Sign fan commands on your computer with HMAC-SHA256, write HMAC from scratch for MicroPython, and make the Pico W accept a command only if the signature, device, command, and sequence number all check out, logging every decision.

m6-l3.title: Practice: break and fix command verifiers, replay guards, and access rules
m6-l3.summary: Find the holes in a broken command handler, show how a missing separator lets two messages share a signature, bound a nonce cache safely, recover a counter after a reboot, check broker access rules, and read an audit log for signs of attack.

m7-l1.title: Keep secrets out of your code and plan for every failure before it happens
m7-l1.summary: Move passwords and keys into a git-ignored secrets file, rotate keys with key IDs, draw the whole system with its trust boundaries, list what happens when each part fails, and reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter.
m7-l1.module: Protect secrets and plan for failure

m7-l2.title: Make the station survive outages with a secrets file, an outbox, and backoff
m7-l2.summary: Split the station into files with secrets kept apart, test a bounded outbox and a jittered backoff timer on your computer, then give the Pico W a connection state machine that keeps sampling through Wi-Fi and broker outages, resubscribes, and flushes oldest first.

m7-l3.title: Practice: scan for leaked secrets, tune backoff, and review a whole design
m7-l3.summary: Write a small secret scanner, reason about what git really keeps, measure the backoff cap trade-off, keep alarms safe in a full outbox, write a failure-mode table for a new device, review a flawed design, and test a reconnect state machine.

m8-l1.title: Plan a secure monitoring system you can build, test, and defend
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, pick one of five projects at your level, and fill in a plan covering topics, payloads, commands, secrets, threats, and failures, checked by a small script before you write any device code.

m8-l2.title: Build the capstone in six milestones from a tested starter
m8-l2.summary: Start from a shared config file and a tested logic module with commands that take arguments, then build sensors, publishing, the dashboard, signed remote actions, resilience, and documentation one working milestone at a time.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your monitoring system, then grade it with the rubric
m8-l3.summary: Write a test plan that covers normal use, boundaries, failures, and attacks, generate a full set of attack messages for your own station, polish the project for someone else to use, run a four-minute demo, and score the result with the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Set up Colab, an Edge Impulse project, and an optional board
m1-l1.summary: Open a Google Colab notebook, create a free Edge Impulse project with your phone connected as a sensor, and, if you have one, prepare an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense or a micro:bit V2.
m1-l1.module: Get set up for TinyML

m1-l2.title: Your first run: fake a sensor, train a one-rule model, and weigh it
m1-l2.summary: Check every library in Colab, chart a synthetic accelerometer signal, train a tiny shake detector with scikit-learn, measure its size in bytes, then record a real sample from your phone in Edge Impulse.

m1-l3.title: Save your work, protect sensor data, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Learn what Colab keeps and what it forgets, organize your notebooks and Edge Impulse projects, treat sensor recordings as personal data, handle boards safely, and fix the errors that stop most people.

m2-l1.title: Decide where a model runs by counting milliseconds, bytes, and joules
m2-l1.summary: Compare on-device and cloud inference by calculating latency, daily data volume, and battery life, weigh privacy, cost, and connectivity, and apply a decision flow to wake words, fall detection, and a wildlife camera.

m2-l2.title: Build an edge-or-cloud calculator for three real products
m2-l2.summary: Describe a smart speaker, a fall-detection pendant, and a wildlife camera as numbers, then build a Python calculator that works out latency, data per day, battery life, and cloud cost for each and recommends edge, cloud, or a cascade with its reasons.

m2-l3.title: Practice: data rates, deadlines, cascades, and battery budgets
m2-l3.summary: Seven exercises and a challenge on choosing edge or cloud inference, from sensor data rates and latency deadlines to false-positive costs in a cascade, battery budgets, unit bugs, data minimization, and packing a report into 7 bytes.

m3-l1.title: Slice a sensor stream into windows, and pick the right task type
m3-l1.summary: Choose a sampling rate that avoids aliasing, cut a continuous accelerometer stream into overlapping windows with a window size and stride, label each window, compute time and frequency features, and decide between classification, anomaly detection, and regression.
m3-l1.module: Prepare sensor windows and task types

m3-l2.title: Build a gesture dataset from raw motion and train a classifier that fits in 400 bytes
m3-l2.summary: Generate 40 synthetic accelerometer recordings of four gestures, cut them into overlapping 2-second windows, extract 15 features per window, split by recording, and compare three classifiers on accuracy and size before setting up the same pipeline in Edge Impulse.

m3-l3.title: Practice: windows, labels, aliasing, leakage, anomalies, and step counting
m3-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on preparing sensor data, from counting windows and dropping mixed-label windows to catching aliasing, building tilt-proof features, exposing leakage, detecting a failing motor with k-means, and estimating walking cadence with regression.

m4-l1.title: Turn sound into spectrograms and MFCCs, then shrink a model to int8
m4-l1.summary: Cut one second of audio into short frames, build a spectrogram, a log-mel spectrogram, and MFCCs with NumPy, see how keyword spotting uses them, and quantize float32 weights to int8 by hand with a scale and zero point.

m4-l2.title: Build a tiny keyword spotter, then quantize it to int8 by hand
m4-l2.summary: Generate 600 one-second clips of two synthetic keywords plus unknown sounds and noise, turn them into MFCCs with NumPy, train a 3,780-parameter 1D CNN in PyTorch, then quantize its weights and inputs to int8 with your own scale and zero-point code and measure accuracy and size at every bit width.

m4-l3.title: Practice: audio frames, pitch, mel spacing, memory budgets, and int8 arithmetic
m4-l3.summary: Seven exercises and a challenge on audio features and quantization, from counting MFCC frames and reading pitch off a spectrogram to checking flash budgets, testing a quantizer against PyTorch, handling outliers, choosing symmetric or asymmetric ranges, and computing a layer with integers only.

m5-l1.title: Count the flash, RAM, and clock cycles a model needs
m5-l1.summary: Count a model's parameters, activation memory, and multiply-accumulates by hand and with PyTorch, and see which limit each one hits on a 64 MHz chip with 1 MB of flash and 256 KB of RAM.

m5-l2.title: Build a flash, RAM, and latency budget for a gesture remote
m5-l2.summary: Profile three candidate gesture models in PyTorch, time them with time.perf_counter, estimate their speed on an nRF52840, and fit the winner into a budget table that counts the whole firmware.

m5-l3.title: Practice: budget a keyword spotter, a camera, and a skip connection
m5-l3.summary: Count parameters, peak RAM, and MACs for audio and image models, fix a broken timing harness, and find the limits that decide what fits on a 256 KB microcontroller.

m6-l1.title: Deploy with Edge Impulse, then measure accuracy where the device lives
m6-l1.summary: Learn what each Edge Impulse deployment option builds, check that the board agrees with Studio, and see with a confusion matrix how a change in sensor placement turns a 98% model into a coin flip for some classes.

m6-l2.title: Build a field-test logger and score it with a confusion matrix
m6-l2.summary: Add ground-truth markers and CSV logging to an Edge Impulse Arduino sketch, then turn the logs from three testers into per-class recall, per-person accuracy, an honest confidence interval, and on-device latency.

m6-l3.title: Practice: read confusion matrices, catch drift, and size a field test
m6-l3.summary: Compute recall and precision from confusion matrices, expose an accuracy number that hides a failing class, run a parity check, find the feature that drifted, and work out how many field blocks you need.

m7-l1.title: Battery math, sleep modes, and what still leaks when data stays on the device
m7-l1.summary: Turn currents and timings into battery life, see why sleep current sets the ceiling for duty-cycled devices, and list what on-device inference protects and what it doesn't.

m7-l2.title: Plan the battery life and data policy of a wildlife camera
m7-l2.summary: Build a calculator that compares four trail-camera designs by battery life and by what data leaves the device, then write the on-device summary that keeps hikers and rare animals private.

m7-l3.title: Practice: battery budgets, wake intervals, and data that says too much
m7-l3.summary: Work out average current and battery life for always-on and duty-cycled devices, solve for the wake interval that hits a one-year target, find which change helps most, and strip a device's messages down to what their purpose needs.

m8-l1.title: Pick a constrained edge-AI device and write its design brief
m8-l1.summary: Choose one of five capstone devices, scope it in four sentences, turn its needs into measurable targets, and start a design doc that every later number will live in.
m8-l1.module: Capstone: a constrained edge-AI device plan

m8-l2.title: Build the device plan milestone by milestone, with a starter notebook
m8-l2.summary: Work through six milestones with a starter notebook that turns your spec, budget, field results, power model, and data-flow table into one scorecard with pass, fail, and estimate labels.

m8-l3.title: Test, tune, present, and grade your device plan
m8-l3.summary: Run the final tests, tune the decision threshold against your precision and recall targets, polish the design doc, present it in five minutes, and check it against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Set up Google Colab and check your library versions
m1-l1.summary: Create a Colab notebook that saves to your own Drive, run a version check, upgrade scikit-learn when Colab's copy is too old, and fix the problems that stop people on day one.
m1-l1.module: Set up a reproducible workspace

m1-l2.title: Make results repeatable with seeds, then prove your toolkit works
m1-l2.summary: Find every source of randomness in a scikit-learn workflow, pin it with random_state, learn why an integer seed and a RandomState object behave differently, measure how much a score moves between seeds, and run a smoke test of the whole toolkit.

m1-l3.title: Organize a project notebook, log every experiment, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Use one notebook template for every project, record each experiment in a CSV log, keep files from vanishing when Colab recycles your runtime, and read scikit-learn's most common errors from the bottom up.

m2-l1.title: Put feature engineering inside the pipeline
m2-l1.summary: Learn the fit/transform contract, route mixed-type columns through a ColumnTransformer, write features as FunctionTransformer steps and custom transformer classes, and watch target encoding done outside the pipeline invent accuracy from a column with no signal.

m2-l2.title: Build-along: a churn pipeline that scores raw rows
m2-l2.summary: Grow a streaming-service churn model from raw columns to engineered features (tenure, viewing per device, an interaction, and a learned age gap), each added as a pipeline step and checked with cross-validation, then score brand-new raw rows and package the model for reuse.

m2-l3.title: Practice: transformers, encoders, and leaks in pipelines
m2-l3.summary: Catch columns a ColumnTransformer silently drops, predict how encoders treat unseen and rare categories, encode clock time on a circle, write a stateful clipping transformer, expose an imputer that peeks at the label, and model a skewed target on the log scale.

m3-l1.title: Pick the cross-validation scheme your data needs
m3-l1.summary: See how much one random split can swing a model comparison, then choose between KFold, StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold, and TimeSeriesSplit by the structure of your data, report several metrics with their fold-to-fold spread, and use nested cross-validation when tuning is part of the model.

m3-l2.title: Build-along: a validation harness that catches a patient-level leak
m3-l2.summary: Build a reusable cross-validation harness, use it to show that shuffling rows from repeat patients flips which model looks best, prove the group-aware folds are clean, and estimate tuned models honestly with nested cross-validation that respects groups.

m3-l3.title: Practice: splitters, scorers, and honest comparisons
m3-l3.summary: Count the fits in a nested search, match splitters to data, explain NaN fold scores, validate a forecast with time-ordered folds and a gap, score models by business cost, use out-of-fold predictions correctly, compare two models across repeated folds, and measure the optimism of a tuned score.

m4-l1.title: Tune hyperparameters on a compute budget
m4-l1.summary: Count what a search costs before running it, see why random search beats a grid when few settings matter, sample on log scales, let successive halving and early stopping cut the work, and watch repeated searching overfit the validation folds.

m4-l2.title: Build-along: tune a boosted churn model inside a time budget
m4-l2.summary: Set a time budget, let early stopping pick the number of trees, run a sized randomized search over a pipeline, read the search results for edge effects and plateaus, check fold by fold whether tuning really helped, and open the test set once.

m4-l3.title: Practice: search spaces, budgets, and stopping rules
m4-l3.summary: Search over whole model families in one grid, predict what scipy distributions actually sample, pick the simplest model within one standard error, compare learning rates under early stopping, predict halving rounds, widen a range whose winner sits on the edge, and measure what tuning on the test set costs.

m5-l1.title: When positives are rare: weights, thresholds, and model ensembles
m5-l1.summary: See why ROC AUC stays calm while a rare-class model floods you with false alarms, learn what class_weight and resampling actually change, set a threshold from the cost of each mistake, and combine models with voting and stacking.
m5-l1.module: Handle rare classes and combine models

m5-l2.title: Build an ensemble that finds rare handwritten 8s
m5-l2.summary: Turn the digits dataset into a rare-class problem, compare four very different models on shared folds, test class weights, combine the models with soft voting and stacking, tune the threshold for recall, and open the test set once.

m5-l3.title: Practice: weights, resampling leaks, cost thresholds, and ensembles that backfire
m5-l3.summary: Compute class weights by hand, catch a resampling leak that inflates AP fourfold, pick a threshold from error costs, explain where hard and soft voting disagree, watch a weak member sink a vote, and test undersampling with bagging.

m6-l1.title: Forests, boosting, and features that secretly know the answer
m6-l1.summary: See how bagging cuts variance and boosting cuts bias, watch boosting fix its own residuals step by step, stop it early, learn why built-in feature importances crown a serial number, and separate target leakage from train-test contamination.
m6-l1.module: Compare forests and boosting, and catch leaks

m6-l2.title: Race a forest against boosting, and catch the two leaks that rig the result
m6-l2.summary: Compare a random forest and histogram gradient boosting on a customer-cancellation export, discover a column recorded after the outcome, find customers who sit on both sides of every split, and rerun the race honestly to see the winner change.

m6-l3.title: Practice: tree ensembles, importance traps, and leaks in disguise
m6-l3.summary: Find where a forest stops improving with out-of-bag scores, trade learning rate against rounds, diagnose bias and variance, watch a duplicated feature hide its importance, and catch leaks hiding in target encoding and shuffled time series.

m7-l1.title: Trustworthy probabilities, honest explanations, and the slices where models fail
m7-l1.summary: Read reliability diagrams and the Brier score, recalibrate a model with CalibratedClassifierCV, explain a model with permutation importance, partial dependence, and ICE curves, and find the subgroups where its errors pile up.

m7-l2.title: Break a tie between two models with calibration, explanations, and error slices
m7-l2.summary: Two late-return models for a library score almost the same ROC AUC. Check their calibration and fix one, compare what each relies on with permutation importance and partial dependence, find the slice where one quietly fails, and confirm the choice once on the test set.

m7-l3.title: Practice: calibration curves, explanation traps, and slices that lie
m7-l3.summary: Compute a Brier score and a reliability table by hand, watch isotonic calibration overfit a small set, catch permutation importance computed on training data, reveal an interaction that partial dependence hides, see why the worst of many slices always looks bad, and undo class weighting with a one-line correction.

m8-l1.title: Capstone brief: plan a model comparison that survives a skeptical reviewer
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, pick one of five projects at different difficulty levels, write a one-page plan that fixes your metric, folds, budget, and decision rule before you see any results, and estimate your compute cost.

m8-l2.title: Capstone build: a starter notebook in nine milestones
m8-l2.summary: Build the comparison report milestone by milestone on the diabetes project, from a sealed test set and nested tuning to a corrected paired test, a cost-based threshold, calibration, leak checks, slices, one look at the test set, and a report drafted from the numbers.

m8-l3.title: Capstone finish: test the evaluation, write it up, present it, and keep going
m8-l3.summary: Put your evaluation code under unit tests, turn metrics into sentences a decision-maker can act on, plan a five-slide presentation, grade the report against the rubric, reflect on what you'd do differently, and pick a next step.

m1-l1.title: Open Colab and switch on a free GPU
m1-l1.summary: Create a Google Colab notebook, attach a free T4 GPU, confirm PyTorch can see it, and fix the problems that stop most people on day one.
m1-l1.module: Set up Colab with a free GPU

m1-l2.title: Move tensors and models to the GPU without device errors
m1-l2.summary: Write the one-line device check that starts every notebook in this course, move models and batches with .to(device), bring results back for NumPy and plotting, and time GPU code without fooling yourself.

m1-l3.title: Save weights, repeat runs exactly, and shrink bugs before you fix them
m1-l3.summary: Learn what survives a Colab disconnect, save and reload model weights in Google Drive, seed your runs so they repeat, lay out notebooks that survive a restart, and debug with a shape, dtype, and device checklist.

m2-l1.title: Tensors, shapes, and the layers that change them
m2-l1.summary: Read a tensor's shape, dtype, and device; reshape and broadcast without scrambling data; see exactly what nn.Linear computes; and learn why ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh exist and where they stop learning.

m2-l2.title: Build a layer-by-layer tracer for a digit classifier
m2-l2.summary: Turn scikit-learn's 8×8 digit images into a batch, build a small PyTorch network for them, follow the batch through it shape by shape, and build a reusable tracer with forward hooks that catches a saturated layer before you train.

m2-l3.title: Practice: predict shapes, count weights, and find flat activations
m2-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on broadcasting, flattening, parameter counts, NaN-free standardization, channel order, and dead or saturated units, each with a hint and a worked solution.

m3-l1.title: Losses, gradients, and the chain rule behind backpropagation
m3-l1.summary: Pick between mean squared error and cross-entropy, compute a one-neuron gradient by hand and confirm it with autograd, then watch gradient descent cross a loss surface and see exactly when a learning rate is too large.

m3-l2.title: Train a logistic neuron with gradients you derive yourself
m3-l2.summary: Derive the gradient of a sigmoid neuron with cross-entropy, prove it correct with autograd and a finite-difference check, train it by hand on a loss surface you can see, sweep the learning rate, and then hand the loop to torch.optim.

m3-l3.title: Practice: compute losses, derive gradients, and choose a step size
m3-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on numerically stable cross-entropy, the softmax-before-loss bug, hand-derived tanh gradients, manual updates under no_grad, the largest stable learning rate, and why classifiers don't use squared error, ending with backpropagation through a two-layer network by hand.

m4-l1.title: Training loops, eval mode, and how to read the curves
m4-l1.summary: Feed data with Dataset and DataLoader, wrap the five-line update in epochs, switch correctly between train and eval mode, log honest per-epoch numbers for training and validation, and read the curves for overfitting and learning-rate trouble.

m4-l2.title: Train a digit classifier with honest curves and a best checkpoint
m4-l2.summary: Split the digits three ways, run two sanity checks before training, train a small network with per-epoch train and validation logging, keep the best checkpoint, plot real learning curves, and score the test set exactly once.

m4-l3.title: Practice: debug training loops and diagnose learning curves
m4-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on starting losses, honest epoch averages, a sneaky accuracy bug, a loop with two silent bugs, predicting curves before you train, early stopping, and a learning-rate range test, ending with beating an overfitting network without more data.

m5-l1.title: Convolutions by hand, plus stride, padding, and pooling
m5-l1.summary: Compute a convolution by hand, predict output sizes from kernel, stride, and padding, see why shared weights and pooling cope with shifted images, and pick augmentations that keep labels true.

m5-l2.title: Build a CNN that still reads digits after they move
m5-l2.summary: Train a small CNN and an MLP on the 8×8 digits with the same loop, test both on shifted copies of the test set, close the gap with per-image augmentation, and look at the filters the CNN learned.

m5-l3.title: Practice CNN shapes, hand-made kernels, and label-safe augmentation
m5-l3.summary: Six exercises and a challenge on output sizes with dilation, parameter budgets, kernel design, a classic shape crash, stress-testing a trained CNN, and writing your own augmentation.

m6-l1.title: Transfer learning, and what detection and segmentation models output
m6-l1.summary: Reuse an ImageNet-trained ResNet by freezing its backbone and replacing its head, decide how much to fine-tune, and read the outputs of detection and segmentation models, scoring boxes with IoU.

m6-l2.title: Fine-tune ResNet-18 on 102 flower species, smoke-tested on CPU first
m6-l2.summary: Build a two-phase transfer-learning script for Oxford Flowers-102 (train the new head, then unfreeze the last stage), checking every piece on a CPU with a sample photo and fake data before spending GPU time.

m6-l3.title: Practice freezing, IoU, NMS, and testing whether transfer pays off
m6-l3.summary: Exercises on choosing what to freeze, the BatchNorm trap, IoU and non-maximum suppression written from scratch, segmentation metrics that don't hide small objects, and an experiment where transfer learning loses.

m7-l1.title: Reproducible runs, GPU memory, and evaluation that shows who the model fails
m7-l1.summary: Record runs so anyone can repeat them, estimate GPU memory before you hit out-of-memory errors, understand mixed precision, and evaluate a vision model by class and by subgroup, with Gender Shades as the case study.
m7-l1.module: Experiment tracking, GPU resources, and evaluation

m7-l2.title: Log a small sweep, then audit the winning model
m7-l2.summary: Write an experiment runner that logs every epoch to CSV, sweep four configurations, pick a winner on validation, and audit it on the test set with a confusion matrix, a failure gallery, and a subgroup table with confidence intervals.

m7-l3.title: Practice memory budgets, reproducibility tests, and honest metrics
m7-l3.summary: Exercises on estimating training memory and batch size, proving gradient accumulation matches a big batch, catching an unseeded random call, reading a confusion matrix, and sizing a subgroup test set.

m8-l1.title: Plan a responsible computer-vision model study
m8-l1.summary: Read the capstone brief, pick one of five projects at different levels, document your dataset, and fill in a one-page plan with a compute budget and five milestones before writing any training code.
m8-l1.module: Capstone: a responsible vision model study

m8-l2.title: Build the study in five milestones from a tested starter
m8-l2.summary: Work through a complete, runnable capstone starter (data and datasheet, a logged baseline, experiments with seeds, a condition-by-condition audit, and a generated model card), then adapt it to your own project.

m8-l3.title: Test, document, and present your vision study
m8-l3.summary: Add six automated tests that catch the classic vision-pipeline bugs, write a model card with specific limitations, present the study in five minutes, grade it against the rubric, and choose what to learn next.

m1-l1.title: Set up Colab with transformers, scikit-learn, and an optional GPU
m1-l1.summary: Create a Colab notebook in your Drive, confirm the NLP libraries are installed and new enough, switch to a GPU runtime when you want one, and store an optional Hugging Face token safely.
m1-l1.module: Set up your NLP workspace

m1-l2.title: Run your first Hugging Face model and prove your setup works
m1-l2.summary: Turn three messages into word counts with scikit-learn, download a tokenizer and a named-entity model from the Hugging Face Hub, run it on your own sentences, and finish with a check cell that proves everything works.

m1-l3.title: Keep notebooks reproducible, private, and easy to debug
m1-l3.summary: Learn what each kind of Colab reset keeps and loses, organize one notebook per lesson, save files that must outlive the runtime, make results repeatable with seeds, read tracebacks from the bottom up, and decide what text is safe to put in a notebook.

m2-l1.title: From raw text to vectors: normalization, tokens, subwords, and embeddings
m2-l1.summary: Decide which strings should count as the same, split text into tokens and subword pieces, and compare four ways of turning tokens into numbers, from one-hot vectors to embeddings.

m2-l2.title: Build a BPE tokenizer and learn word vectors from co-occurrence
m2-l2.summary: Train a byte-pair-encoding tokenizer from scratch on 18 sentences, turn text into padded id sequences, then learn word vectors from a co-occurrence table with SVD and plot where "bank" lands between its two meanings.

m2-l3.title: Practice: tokenizers, vocabularies, and TF-IDF by hand
m2-l3.summary: Measure out-of-vocabulary rates, see what bigrams add to a bag of words, write a regex tokenizer for prices and emails, rebuild TF-IDF with NumPy, pad and truncate a batch, chart BPE compression, and finish by writing a WordPiece tokenizer.

m3-l1.title: Compare texts with cosine similarity and label them with classifiers
m3-l1.summary: Measure how alike two texts are with cosine similarity, build a small search over past tickets, train naive Bayes and logistic regression to label new ones, and read accuracy, precision, recall, and a confusion matrix honestly.

m3-l2.title: Build a support-ticket triage tool with a classifier and similar-case search
m3-l2.summary: Label 60 realistic support tickets with a TF-IDF and logistic regression pipeline, find out why the first version fails, improve it with evidence from cross-validation, chart the confusion matrix, add similar-case search, and send low-confidence tickets to a human.

m3-l3.title: Practice: similarity search, classifier metrics, and honest evaluation
m3-l3.summary: Find near-duplicate tickets, compute precision and recall by hand, catch a misleading accuracy score, measure how much cross-validation scores wobble, make search survive typos, chart the coverage-accuracy trade-off, and build a nearest-neighbour classifier yourself.

m4-l1.title: How a transformer labels every token to find names, places, and organizations
m4-l1.summary: Treat named-entity recognition as one label per token with BIO tags, decode tags into entities, see where rules beat models, read what a Hugging Face pipeline returns, and follow a sentence from tokens to ids to logits to labels inside a transformer.

m4-l2.title: Build an entity extractor that combines rules with a transformer, then look inside it
m4-l2.summary: Hand-label 20 entities in four short documents, score a regex extractor and a transformer NER model against them, merge the two into one extractor, then open the model to see the probabilities behind a wrong label and chart what two attention heads look at.

m4-l3.title: Practice: BIO tags, subword labels, logits, and attention by hand
m4-l3.summary: Decode and encode BIO tags, align word labels with subword tokens the way NER training does, compare token-level and span-level scores, turn logits into entities, compute attention weights with and without a causal mask, and finish with a tested redaction tool.

m5-l1.title: Compute attention by hand, and see why context runs out
m5-l1.summary: Build scaled dot-product attention in NumPy one matrix at a time, mask the future the way GPT does, see why word order needs positions, and work out what a context window really limits.

m5-l2.title: Build a context planner that never drops a definition silently
m5-l2.summary: Estimate tokens, budget a 512-token window, watch plain truncation lose the part of a policy that matters, then pin, rank, and pack sections so the prompt fits and reports what it left out.

m5-l3.title: Practice: attention weights, masks, heads, and token budgets
m5-l3.summary: Write a softmax that can't overflow, read attention weights, build a causal mask and a two-head attention layer, then budget a long chat and reorder chunks so key facts don't get lost in the middle.

m6-l1.title: Write prompts as code, demand a schema, and ground answers in retrieved text
m6-l1.summary: Build prompts from templates with clear rules and few-shot examples, validate model output against a JSON Schema and a Pydantic model, and see how retrieval plus citation checks keeps answers tied to real sources.

m6-l2.title: Build a retrieval pipeline that checks every citation
m6-l2.summary: Chunk a small library help center with overlap, retrieve with TF-IDF, build a grounded prompt with numbered sources, and reject any reply that fails the schema or cites a source it was never shown.

m6-l3.title: Practice: parse replies, enforce schemas, pick examples, and test retrieval
m6-l3.summary: Pull JSON out of messy model replies, write the same contract as a JSON Schema and a Pydantic model, choose balanced few-shot examples, chunk with overlap, measure retrieval hit rate, and defend a prompt against injected instructions.

m7-l1.title: Catch hallucinations, score answers, and choose how to adapt a model
m7-l1.summary: Sort hallucinations into types, run grounding checks that catch changed numbers and unsupported claims, score answers with exact match and token F1, and decide between prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, and LoRA.

m7-l2.title: Build an evaluation harness that decides if a Q&A bot can launch
m7-l2.summary: Write an eval set with unanswerable questions, score two systems on answer quality, citations, invented numbers, unsupported claims, abstention, and privacy leaks, then let a launch gate say pass or fail with reasons.

m7-l3.title: Practice: scoring answers, checking quantities, and choosing how to adapt
m7-l3.summary: Compare exact match and F1 on tricky pairs, catch wrong units and rates, measure abstention, size LoRA adapters, pick an adaptation strategy, put error bars on a small eval, and test whether an LLM judge can be trusted.

m8-l1.title: Plan a grounded question-answering system for documents you choose
m8-l1.summary: Pick one of five project ideas, choose documents that are safe to use, fill in a one-page plan, and write the output schema and evaluation set before any pipeline code exists.

m8-l2.title: Build the grounded Q&A system in six milestones
m8-l2.summary: Work through a runnable starter, from ingesting and scrubbing files to chunking, retrieval with a measured hit rate, budgeted prompts, checks that force abstention, and an evaluation gate, then swap in your own documents and a real model.

m8-l3.title: Test, document, and present your Q&A system
m8-l3.summary: Write unit tests for the parts that must never break, add adversarial cases to the eval set, write a limits statement, give a five-minute presentation that shows a failure, and grade the project against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Set up Colab and a research project folder you can rerun
m1-l1.summary: Create a Colab notebook backed by Google Drive, lay out a project folder that separates raw data from everything derived from it, and record the exact library versions in a requirements file.
m1-l1.module: Set up a reproducible research workspace

m1-l2.title: Run a seeded first experiment and prove it reruns exactly
m1-l2.summary: Simulate a small greenhouse experiment from a fixed seed, fingerprint the data file with SHA-256, estimate the treatment effect with statsmodels, save a run record, and show that rerunning reproduces every number.

m1-l3.title: Keep a research log, protect your data, and get unstuck
m1-l3.summary: Work the way this course expects. Keep a dated research log, prove notebooks with Restart session and run all, de-identify data about people, draw charts everyone can read, and shrink any error to a small example someone can help with.

m2-l1.title: Turn a research hunch into a question a model can answer
m2-l1.summary: Rewrite a vague idea as a testable question with a population, inputs, comparison, outcome, and success threshold; tell prediction questions from explanation questions; and read a paper's claims, data, baselines, metrics, and effect sizes like a referee.
m2-l1.module: Frame questions and read papers critically

m2-l2.title: Build an evidence table that checks papers against their own numbers
m2-l2.summary: Turn a research question into a structured plan, enter what six studies report, compute the confidence intervals, majority-class baselines, and effect sizes they left out, flag weak evidence automatically, and plot everything on one scale.

m2-l3.title: Practice: sharpen research questions and stress-test reported results
m2-l3.summary: Rewrite vague questions until they can fail, sort prediction goals from causal ones, and recompute base rates, confidence intervals, and effect sizes that papers leave out.

m3-l1.title: Audit where your data came from before a model learns its quirks
m3-l1.summary: Ask the provenance questions every dataset needs, read missing values as a pattern, spot batch effects with PCA, see why a confounded design can't be fixed by analysis, and size an experiment with a power calculation.

m3-l2.title: Audit a three-greenhouse dataset, then design the experiment that fixes it
m3-l2.summary: Audit a pilot dataset of leaf spectra from three greenhouses for provenance, independent units, missingness, and site fingerprints; show that a model's score collapses on a new greenhouse; then lay out a randomized, blocked, controlled follow-up and size it with a power analysis.

m3-l3.title: Practice: find the flaw in the data before the model does
m3-l3.summary: Diagnose missingness in wearable data, correct plate-to-plate drift with reference wells, redesign a confounded layout, size experiments and test sets with power analysis, and rebuild a famous dataset flaw to see a near-perfect model fail.

m4-l1.title: Beat the simplest baseline before you trust a complex model
m4-l1.summary: Climb a baseline ladder from dummy models to a one-feature rule, a linear model, and only then a forest or neural network; measure how much scores move between seeds; and list everything beyond the seed that a rerun needs.

m4-l2.title: Build a baseline ladder and an experiment that reruns in one call
m4-l2.summary: Predict enzyme melting temperatures from sequence descriptors with a five-rung baseline ladder scored on held-out assay batches, then package the whole experiment as one function that writes a run record, reruns identically, and passes a reproducibility checklist.

m4-l3.title: Practice: baselines, seed spread, and results someone else can rerun
m4-l3.summary: Climb a classification ladder on a medical dataset, decide whether a small gain survives a change of seed, catch edited data and drifted environments by fingerprint, audit run records, hunt down hidden randomness, and try to reproduce a number from an incomplete methods section.

m5-l1.title: Put a range on every number: standard errors, bootstrap intervals, and prediction intervals
m5-l1.summary: See how much a test score wobbles from sample to sample, then compute standard errors, bootstrap confidence intervals by hand and with scipy.stats.bootstrap, and prediction intervals for new measurements.

m5-l2.title: Build an uncertainty report for a model comparison
m5-l2.summary: Compare a baseline, logistic regression, and a random forest on a simulated lake survey using repeated cross-validation, a corrected interval for paired fold differences, and bootstrap intervals on a locked test set, then turn the numbers into a figure and one reportable sentence.

m5-l3.title: Intervals for medians, correlations, mice, AUCs, and new predictions
m5-l3.summary: Decode reported error bars, bootstrap differences, correlations, and clustered measurements correctly, put an interval on a test-set AUC, build a prediction interval for any model, and check whether a 95% interval really covers 95% of the time.

m6-l1.title: When a score is too good: leakage, ablations, and sensitivity checks
m6-l1.summary: Watch KFold and GroupKFold give very different scores on the same data, catch time leakage with forward-chaining splits, run an ablation that exposes a shortcut feature, and test whether conclusions survive other seeds, hyperparameters, and the number of analyses you tried.

m6-l2.title: Audit a multi-site soil study: leakage check, ablation table, and sensitivity sweep
m6-l2.summary: Build a leak-proof pipeline with custom batch-correction and index steps, compare row-level and site-level cross-validation, run an ablation with error bars, sweep a hyperparameter across seeds, and assemble the results into an audit table and a methods-ready paragraph.

m6-l3.title: Find the leak, test the seed, correct the count
m6-l3.summary: Choose splitters for real study designs, catch oversampling and rolling-window leaks, test a claimed gain against seed noise, correct fifteen p-values three ways, expose redundant components in an ablation, block a spatial dataset, and measure the optimism of non-nested tuning.

m7-l1.title: Reproduce, then report: matching a paper, explaining the gaps, and writing it up
m7-l1.summary: Tell reproduction from replication, choose a result you can actually check, decide in advance what counts as a match, test whether a gap is bigger than sampling error, keep a discrepancy log, and write methods, limitations, and figures that hold up, using the REFORMS checklist.

m7-l2.title: Reproduce a 1992 wine-classifier comparison and write it up
m7-l2.summary: Take the leave-one-out accuracies reported for the UCI wine data, pre-register what counts as a match, audit the dataset's provenance, reproduce LDA, QDA, and 1-nearest-neighbor results, investigate a one-sample discrepancy without fishing, and generate a reproduction report with intervals, a discrepancy log, and limitations.

m7-l3.title: Judge reproductions, catch impossible numbers, and write it up honestly
m7-l3.summary: Classify reproduction attempts, test whether a gap exceeds sampling error at two test-set sizes, catch impossible reported percentages, rewrite a vague methods paragraph, redraw a misleading figure, audit a paper with REFORMS, test whether a reproduced ranking is robust, and diff two pipelines to find the leak behind a failed reproduction.

m8-l1.title: Plan your capstone: a published-result reproduction study
m8-l1.summary: Choose a published result to reproduce from five options at different difficulty levels, check that it's precise enough to test, and fill in a pre-registration plan with the claim, match rule, primary analysis, controls, uncertainty, sensitivity checks, and what you won't attempt.

m8-l2.title: Build your reproduction in six milestones, worked through on ESL's cross-validation trap
m8-l2.summary: Work through every capstone milestone on a real published result (the "wrong way to cross-validate" simulation from ESL Section 7.10.2), including a declared ambiguity, positive and negative controls, intervals over simulations, a secondary claim that resolves the ambiguity, built-in tests, and a generated report, then adapt the starter skeleton to your own target.

m8-l3.title: Test, polish, and present your reproduction study
m8-l3.summary: Run the checks a reviewer will run, lint your figures automatically, structure the report and a five-minute talk, grade yourself against the rubric, and decide where to share the finished reproduction.

m1-l1.title: Install Python 3.12, Docker, and Git for model deployment
m1-l1.summary: Install the three tools every module uses (Python 3.12, Docker, and Git with a GitHub account) on Windows, macOS, or Linux, or open a free GitHub Codespace on a Chromebook, and check each one from a terminal.
m1-l1.module: Set up your MLOps workstation

m1-l2.title: Create the project, pin its libraries, and prove the toolchain works
m1-l2.summary: Make the late-delivery project folder and a Python 3.12 virtual environment, install exact library versions, then pass three checks: a model that survives save and reload, an API that answers /health, and a container running Python 3.12.

m1-l3.title: Organize the project, commit safely, and debug the errors you'll meet
m1-l3.summary: Scaffold the late-delivery project layout, decide what belongs in Git, keep Docker from filling your disk, and learn a routine for reading tracebacks, HTTP errors, and container failures.

m2-l1.title: Turn a trained model into a service with a contract
m2-l1.summary: Save the whole scikit-learn pipeline as an artifact, describe valid requests with Pydantic, serve predictions from FastAPI with the model loaded once at startup, and decide which status code every failure deserves.

m2-l2.title: Build, test, and containerize the late-delivery API
m2-l2.summary: Generate the training data, train and save the model with a metadata file, write the FastAPI service and its tests, then build a Docker image that runs as a non-root user with a health check, and call it with curl.

m2-l3.title: Harden the prediction service: contracts, health checks, batches, and logs
m2-l3.summary: Tighten an API contract that accepts nonsense, make the health check honest, add a batch endpoint and structured request logs, review a broken Dockerfile, and measure what loading a model per request really costs.

m3-l1.title: Batch, online, streaming, or edge: match the serving mode to the job
m3-l1.summary: Compare the four ways to deliver predictions, measure latency percentiles and batch throughput on the course model, size a service with Little's law, estimate costs, and pick a free host that fits each mode.
m3-l1.module: Choose batch, online, streaming, or edge

m3-l2.title: Serve one model two ways: a nightly batch job and a benchmarked online API
m3-l2.summary: Write a chunked batch scorer that stamps every prediction with its model version, benchmark the online API's latency percentiles and chart them, schedule the batch job with GitHub Actions, and deploy the API to Render's free tier.

m3-l3.title: Choose and size serving modes with real numbers
m3-l3.summary: Classify workloads by serving mode, check a latency objective with percentiles, size an API with Little's law, pick a micro-batch size under a latency budget, make a batch job resumable, find a cost break-even, and build a hybrid batch-plus-online lookup.

m4-l1.title: Know exactly which model answered, with versions, hashes, and registry records
m4-l1.summary: Pin down a model by its code, data, configuration, environment, and artifact; fingerprint files with SHA-256, give models semantic versions and moving aliases, write a registry record, and see how MLflow's tracking server and model registry do the same job.
m4-l1.module: Version models, data, and registry records

m4-l2.title: Build a file-based model registry with hashes, aliases, and model cards
m4-l2.summary: Write a small registry that stores immutable model versions with hashed records, tracks a champion alias with a full history, promotes a retrained model only when it holds up on a fixed holdout, refuses to serve a tampered artifact, and generates a model card from the record.

m4-l3.title: Version detective work: fingerprints, lineage, rollbacks, and promotion gates
m4-l3.summary: Decide version bumps, build an order-independent dataset fingerprint, audit a registry record against the files on disk, trace which versions used bad data, find what was serving at an incident's timestamp, write a multi-rule promotion gate, and automate the next version number.

m5-l1.title: Make a training pipeline refuse to ship a bad model
m5-l1.summary: Order pipeline steps so checks run before anything is published, write unit, data, model, and service tests for ML code, and see how GitHub Actions runs them on every push.

m5-l2.title: Build a CI workflow that blocks a weak late-delivery model
m5-l2.summary: Add data tests, behavioral model tests, an API contract snapshot, and a quality gate script to the late-delivery repo, then wire them into a GitHub Actions workflow that only uploads a model when every check passes.

m5-l3.title: Practice CI checks: unit bugs, slice regressions, and flaky gates
m5-l3.summary: Write reference-statistics checks, a dependency-aware pipeline runner, a per-slice quality gate, a contract test that catches a wrong-column bug, and a deploy job that only runs after tests pass.

m6-l1.title: Ship every passing commit safely, then watch what the model does live
m6-l1.summary: Turn CI into continuous deployment, choose between rolling, blue-green, canary, and shadow releases, write health checks that know about the model, and monitor latency, errors, and drift with alert rules that don't cry wolf.

m6-l2.title: Build a monitor that reads the prediction log and raises the right alerts
m6-l2.summary: Log one JSON line per prediction from the late-delivery API, replay a day of traffic with a new delivery zone and a road closure, then compute golden signals, PSI by hand, KS tests, prediction drift, and outcome-based accuracy, and turn them into OK, ticket, or page decisions.

m6-l3.title: Practice monitoring: shadow tests, rolling percentiles, drift traps, and alerts that don't flap
m6-l3.summary: Compare a challenger in shadow mode, compute rolling p99 against an SLO, fix PSI edge cases, avoid the KS sample-size trap, detect concept drift with delayed labels, and build alerts with hysteresis and burn rates.

m7-l1.title: Roll back on evidence, spend on purpose, and run incidents with a plan
m7-l1.summary: Automate canary decisions with sample-size and per-slice checks, roll back by moving a registry alias, reason about cost per prediction and cost limits, and handle incidents with clear roles, a runbook, and a blameless postmortem.
m7-l1.module: Roll back, optimize, and handle incidents

m7-l2.title: Make the late-delivery service faster and cheaper, and prove it with measurements
m7-l2.summary: Benchmark the prediction path, compile the scikit-learn pipeline into a parity-tested NumPy scorer, batch and cache repeated requests, quantize a neural-net challenger to float32 and int8, and turn every measurement into cost per million predictions.

m7-l3.title: Practice rollbacks, costs, and incidents: slice canaries, peeking, TTL caches, and postmortems
m7-l3.summary: Find the slice a canary broke, see why checking a canary every few minutes causes false rollbacks, roll back to the last good registry version, build a TTL cache, cap a cost budget, and turn a raw incident timeline into postmortem numbers.

m8-l1.title: Plan a production-style ML service you could hand to an on-call team
m8-l1.summary: Pick a capstone project at the right difficulty, write a one-page service plan with a contract, SLOs, gates, release and rollback rules, monitoring, a cost budget, and a security list, then size it before writing code.

m8-l2.title: Build the capstone in six milestones, starting from a working skeleton
m8-l2.summary: Start from a runnable skeleton of the late-delivery service (training, a hashed registry, a model-aware API, tests, a gate, Docker, CI/CD, a monitor, and a rollback drill), then replace each piece with your own project one milestone at a time.

m8-l3.title: Test, secure, document, and present your ML service
m8-l3.summary: Run a pre-launch check of load, bad input, failure injection, and a rollback drill; close the common security gaps; write the README, model card, and runbook; present a five-minute demo; and score the project against the rubric.

m1-l1.title: Install Python, Git, VS Code, and an AI coding assistant
